items.name: theme
items.title: Pulse
items.description: The Pulse design tokens - surfaces, accents, foreground and hairlines - as a Tailwind v4 theme, plus the reset the components are drawn against and the Overpass Mono typeface.
items.docs:
The tokens are light-dark() pairs resolved by color-scheme, never a second block of variables
under a media query or a .dark class. Pulse is dark-first: :root sets color-scheme: dark, and
data-theme="light" opts into the light column. Switch themes by setting color-scheme, never by
redefining a token - light-dark() resolves per element, so a subtree with its own color-scheme
flips on its own.

This item also carries Overpass Mono, the only typeface the system uses, at the four weights the
components use. A component item leaves the font out on purpose, so that adding a Button does not
also add a font package; the family falls back to the monospace stack until this item is installed.

items.name: accordion
items.title: Accordion
items.description: The sheet has no accordion in it — the second component here with nothing to copy, after the date picker — so this follows its language rather than its markup: the control step of the radius scale, mono, and the hairline vocabulary of its dividers.
items.docs:
The sheet has no accordion in it — the second component here with nothing to copy, after the date
picker — so this follows its _language_ rather than its markup: the control step of the radius scale,
mono, and the hairline vocabulary of its dividers.

```tsx
<Accordion defaultExpandedKeys={['checks']}>
  <Accordion.Item id="checks">
    <Accordion.Header>Checks</Accordion.Header>
    <Accordion.Panel>Three checks are failing.</Accordion.Panel>
  </Accordion.Item>
  <Accordion.Item id="history">
    <Accordion.Header>History</Accordion.Header>
    <Accordion.Panel>No incidents in the last 24 hours.</Accordion.Panel>
  </Accordion.Item>
</Accordion>
```

| Slot               | React Aria        | Notes                                                           |
| ------------------ | ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Accordion`        | `DisclosureGroup` | The set. Owns which items are open                              |
| `Accordion.Item`   | `Disclosure`      | One row. Its `id` is what `expandedKeys` speaks in              |
| `Accordion.Header` | `Button`          | The whole row, `slot="trigger"`; `indicator` replaces the caret |
| `Accordion.Panel`  | `DisclosurePanel` | The content, hidden while the row is closed                     |

### What it looks like, and why

Three things, all borrowed rather than invented — which is the point, since the sheet has no
accordion to copy:

- **The label is the sheet's row legend**: 12px, uppercase, `tracking-[0.06em]` — the same
  treatment the sheet gives a field legend and a table row. A sentence-case 13px heading reads as
  a different design system entirely, which is what the first version of this component looked
  like.
- **The open row is one panel block.** The sheet's `.ds-panel` surface goes on the whole item, not
  on the body alone, so the heading is part of the block instead of floating above a tinted
  paragraph. Closed rows are plain, separated by the sheet's `.ds-div-hair`.
- **The accent goes on the caret, and nowhere else.** An open row already says so twice without
  colour — the panel surface and the label going from 55% to full strength — so the caret is where
  a little teal does the most work. There was a 2px accent rule down the open row's leading edge
  for a while; it was removed. Three signals for one state was one too many, and a full-height
  rule beside every accordion is a lot of a system's single accent to spend on a disclosure.

All of it is published from the item as custom properties — `--accordion-ink`,
`--accordion-caret-ink`, `--accordion-row-bg`, `--accordion-caret-rotate` — and only _read_
further in: `data-expanded` is on the item, not on the header button, so a rule reaching the
caret through a group variant would tie on specificity and lose.

### The set decides, not the item

By default opening one closes the rest. That is the difference between an accordion and a stack
of independent disclosures — and writing a `Disclosure` per row and calling it an accordion is
how you get the second by accident. `allowsMultipleExpanded` asks for the other behaviour, on
purpose.

`expandedKeys` / `onExpandedChange` speak in the items' `id`s. Uncontrolled use takes
`defaultExpandedKeys`; controlling the set means passing `expandedKeys`, and the component will
not change it for you.

### The whole row is the button

Not the word inside it. A header sized to its label makes an accordion fiddly with a mouse, and
the `Default` story asserts the row is as wide as the set rather than as wide as "History".

### The caret reads a variable from the item

`data-expanded` is on the **item**, while the caret is inside the button inside it — so the
rotation is published as `--accordion-caret-rotate` on the item and read by the caret. Same
arrangement as `Select`, `ComboBox` and the date pickers, same reason: a rule reaching a child
through a group variant ties on specificity and loses on source order.

### A closed panel is hidden, but it still has a box

React Aria leaves it mounted, hidden with `hidden="until-found"` — out of sight and out of the
accessibility tree, but still in the document, which is what lets the browser's find-in-page open
the right one. Two consequences, and the second one is a styling bug that is easy to ship:

1. **A text query still finds it.** `queryByText(...)` is the wrong assertion; `.not.toBeVisible()`
   is the right one. My first version of this component's JSDoc claimed the panel was unmounted,
   which the failing test corrected.
2. **`hidden="until-found"` does not remove the box.** The browser implements it as
   `content-visibility: hidden`, which skips the _content_ but keeps the element's own padding and
   border — and Tailwind's preflight deliberately leaves `[hidden="until-found"]` out of its
   `display: none` rule, so nothing else removes it either. A panel with `pb-4` on it therefore
   added **16px of dead space under every closed row**: each item measured 65px for a 48px
   header. The panel's padding and border are guarded on not being hidden for exactly this reason.

The panel has no `data-expanded` to key off — my first version used one, so the padding and the
top hairline never applied at all. `hidden` is the attribute that is actually there.

Disabled stops a row being _changed_, it does not close what is already shown.

items.title: Avatar
items.description: Who something belongs to — a monitor's owner, an alert's assignee — as a picture or as initials.
items.docs: Who something belongs to — a monitor's owner, an alert's assignee — as a picture or as initials. ```tsx // initials, when there is no picture // a machine's name works the same way ``` | prop | default | notes | | --------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | | `alt` | — | required; a **name**, and it becomes the initials | | `src` | — | omit it, or let it fail, and the initials are used | | `size` | `md` | `sm` 24px, `md` 32px, `lg` 40px | | `color` | `neutral` | `Button`'s five | | `isPreviewable` | `false` | opens the avatar large in a modal; it becomes a button | ## The fourth component with nothing to copy `pulse-replica/` has no avatar, no user chip and nothing person-shaped at all — after the date picker, the accordion and the toast, this is the fourth component here invented rather than replicated. So every decision comes from the system's own language: - **Square by default, and a circle never.** The sheet squares off its controls and makes exactly two exceptions, the checkbox's 2px and the radio's circle; a round avatar would be a **third**, so the box wears the control step of the radius scale — `rounded-md`, which is `0` in the sheet and a soft square under a theme. It is the one place a designer expects a circle, which is why it is stated rather than left to look like an oversight. - **A fill carrying `ink`**, like every other filled control: black on the luminous dark-theme accents, white on the deep light-theme ones. The five colours are literally `Button`'s table, so an avatar cannot drift away from the palette it sits beside. - **Mono, uppercase, letterspaced initials** — the face every other label here wears. ## Initials are derived, and the edges are checked The first letter of the first and last words, or the first two letters of a single word: | `alt` | initials | | ----------------- | -------- | | `Ada Lovelace` | `AL` | | `Ada B. Lovelace` | `AL` | | `fra1` | `FR` | | `" "` | `?` | A middle name does not change it, because the surname is what distinguishes two Adas. A name with no letters at all still has to render something, so it gets `?` rather than an empty box — the one case where the fallback invents rather than derives. A generic silhouette was the alternative and was rejected: it says "somebody", and in a monitoring system _which_ somebody is the entire content of the cell. ## A broken image falls back to initials, not to nothing `onError` swaps the `` for the initials. This is not an edge case — an avatar URL that 404s, a service with no picture, a directory that has not synced — it is the state a real dashboard spends most of its life in, and the failure mode of not handling it is an empty box. `BrokenImage` is a story with a source that cannot load, and it asserts the initials appear and the `` is gone. ## The name is announced once The wrapper is `role="img"` with `aria-label={alt}` and the inner `` is `alt=""`. Giving both a name announces the same person twice; giving only the image one leaves the initials case — the majority case — with no name at all. The `Default` story asserts the picture **actually arrived** by checking `naturalWidth`: an `` in the DOM proves nothing on its own, because a 404 leaves one behind. ## `isPreviewable` changes the element, not the styling ```tsx ``` Off — the default — this is a ``, a picture the tab order correctly skips. On, it is a **real `

items.name: bar-chart
items.title: BarChart
items.description: A histogram — a row of bars over a dot-grid zone, with one of them allowed to be the current one.
items.docs:
A histogram — a row of bars over a dot-grid zone, with one of them allowed to be the current one.

```tsx
<BarChart
  values={[12, 30, 18, 44, 26, 9]}
  labels={['00', '04', '08', '12', '16', '20']}
  highlightIndex={3}
  label="Requests per four hours"
/>
```

| prop             | default | notes                                       |
| ---------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `values`         | —       | one bar each, oldest first                  |
| `labels`         | —       | one per bar, under it; omit for no axis row |
| `highlightIndex` | —       | the bar the page is about                   |
| `width`/`height` | 720/256 | user units **and** rendered px              |
| `label`          | —       | required; the drawing's only text           |

## What `drawBars` actually draws

Copied from `pulse-replica/js/system.js`, which is exactly four things:

1. a **dot-grid zone** across the plotting area — `rgba(255,255,255,.15)` dots, radius `1`, `7.7px` pitch.
   That is a **lighter** texture than the sparkline's `.32`/`0.9`: a bar chart is busy enough without the
   background competing with it.
2. a **baseline rule** — 1px at `rgba(255,255,255,.34)`. This is what makes the bars sit on something
   rather than float.
3. the **bars**, `--chart-1` grey except the flagged one, which is the accent.
4. the **axis row** below: the replica's `.dash-axis`, a relative 24px row with each label absolutely
   positioned under the centre of its bar. Placing them as percentages rather than pixels is what keeps
   them aligned when the chart stretches.

## `highlightIndex` is the replica's `b[3]` flag

This is the reason the component is a _monitoring_ chart rather than a plotting library. The interesting
bar is the one the page is about — the current hour, the breached window, the monitor you clicked — and a
colour that says which one costs nothing.

**Everything else is grey, deliberately.** `.ds-tag` and the segmented control spend the accent on the
thing that is _chosen_; a histogram is the same idea at chart scale, and a chart in which every bar is teal
has stopped saying which bar matters. The `Highlighted` story asserts exactly one accent bar — by counting
fills, not by trusting the prop.

## Two details that were got wrong first

**The `<pattern>` id is `useId`-derived.** The first version hardcoded `bar-chart-dots`. `<pattern>` ids are
document-global, so the second chart on a page would have painted the first one's dots and lost its own
zone the moment that one unmounted. `Sparkline` had already paid for this lesson.

**`--chart-1` is a new token, and it does not invert.** The replica's `--c-bar` is `#686d73` in a
dark-only sheet. Every other colour here is `light-dark(...)` because it carries text; a bar is a _measured
value_, so `ink`'s inversion rule does not apply. It is `oklch(45%)` in light against a white page and
`oklch(52%)` in dark — a mid grey in both.

## A picture, and the numbers belong beside it

The `<svg>` is `role="img"` with one `label`, so a screen reader hears "Requests per four hours" and not the
series. A chart cannot be read out through `role="img"` and this component does not pretend otherwise —
`role="img"` also hides its children from assistive tech, so per-bar `<title>` elements would be ignored.
Where the values are the point, render them as a `Table` next to it. `Sparkline`'s docs record the same
boundary.

## The hover readout, and the assertion that would have caught the zone

`BarChart` shows a value under the pointer, copied from `place()` in `pulse-replica/js/system.js`.
`dashboard.html` keeps a `.dash-tip--chart` panel (`#pc-tip`) and the script positions it on
`pointermove` — **with a tolerance rather than a per-bar event**: a bar whose x-range contains the pointer,
with 2 units of slack, wins outright; otherwise the nearest bar within 14 units is used; otherwise nothing
happens. That tolerance is why the readout feels attached to the chart rather than to a rectangle — a
pointer just past an edge still reads the bar.

The pointer is converted into the drawing's **own user units** before the hit test, exactly as the replica
does. Without that, a stretched chart reads the wrong bar — which is not hypothetical: the first version of
this story's test measured from the wrapper's width while assuming the drawing's 720, and asserted the
fourth bar while pointing at the third.

**It is `aria-hidden`.** A readout that exists only under a pointer is not available to a keyboard, so
announcing it would claim an affordance the component cannot keep. The values belong in a `Table` beside
the chart.

## The dot grid was never painting, and nothing said so

`<pattern id="bar-chart-dots">` kept a **hardcoded** id while the zone referenced `patternId` — a
`useId`-derived value that existed only in the class list. So `fill="url(#bar-chart-dots-…)"` pointed at a
definition that did not exist, and an SVG resolves a broken `url(#…)` to **transparent**: no error, no
warning, no visual difference from a zone that was never meant to be there.

Every assertion passed. They checked the bars, the baseline, the axis and the colours — the zone was checked
only by counting rects, and a rect that paints nothing still exists. There is now an assertion that the id
the zone **asks for** is the id the pattern **defines**, which is the only check that can fail for this.

It was fixed once before and the fix silently did not apply: the patch anchored on a single-line tag that
Prettier had already reflowed. That is the second time in this repo a scripted edit reported success and
changed nothing, and the reason the assertion above exists rather than the line being trusted.

## `drawDemoBars` is covered by this component

The replica has a second histogram function, `drawDemoBars`, and it is worth saying why there is no second
component for it. It draws the same four things as `drawBars` — the dot zone, the baseline rule, the bars,
the accent on one of them — and differs in exactly three numbers:

|             | `drawBars`                       | `drawDemoBars`                     |
| ----------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| bar width   | fills its slot                   | a fixed `12.5`, on a `w / n` pitch |
| bar height  | `v / max` of the plotting height | the same, with a **6px floor**     |
| zone height | to `baseline`                    | to `h - 1`                         |

Those are parameter choices rather than a different drawing, and the floor is the only one with a
consequence: a bar of zero becomes a visible sliver. For a monitoring histogram that is a real ambiguity —
_no data_ and _zero_ look identical either way — and the axis row is what resolves it here, since it names
every bucket whether or not it drew. `drawBars` allows the flat zero and this follows it.

If a page needs the narrow fixed-width strip, that is `BarChart` with more space between bars than the
default `GAP`; it is not a second component.

items.name: breadcrumbs
items.title: Breadcrumbs
items.description: A trail back up the hierarchy, where the last step is the page you are on.
items.docs:
A trail back up the hierarchy, where the last step is the page you are on.

```tsx
<Breadcrumbs label="Breadcrumb">
  <Breadcrumbs.Item href="/monitors">Monitors</Breadcrumbs.Item>
  <Breadcrumbs.Item href="/monitors/fra1">fra1</Breadcrumbs.Item>
  <Breadcrumbs.Item>Frankfurt</Breadcrumbs.Item>
</Breadcrumbs>
```

| Slot               | React Aria    | Notes                                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Breadcrumbs`      | `Breadcrumbs` | The trail. `label` names the `<nav>`                        |
| `Breadcrumbs.Item` | `Breadcrumb`  | One step. `href` makes it a link; without one it is current |

**The sheet has no breadcrumb in it**, so the arrangement is an invention — but every visible part is
borrowed: the sheet's own `.ds-link-caps` for the steps, its softest line tone for the punctuation,
and its muted-to-full-strength hierarchy for the trail above you.

### React Aria renders the list and not the landmark

`Breadcrumbs` is an `<ol>` — **no `<nav>` around it and no role on the list.** The first version of this
component was therefore a list of links sitting in no landmark at all, so a screen reader's landmark
list offered no way to reach it. A breadcrumb _is_ navigation; the wrapper is this component's job, so
`Breadcrumbs` draws the `<nav aria-label>` itself and the `label` prop goes there rather than through
to React Aria.

### The slash is a pseudo-element, and that is right here

It belongs to the item, not to the list, and `last:after:content-none` is what stops a trail ending in
a stray `/`. A pseudo-element is correct for it — a slash carries no text, cannot be pressed and needs
no accessible name — which is exactly why the caret in `Nav` could **not** be one.

### The page you are on has to be visible, and one class was hiding it

React Aria marks the **current** breadcrumb `data-disabled` as well as `data-current` — deliberately,
since the page you are on is not pressable — and the item carried `data-[disabled]:hidden`, meant for
crumbs React Aria never renders. Every trail in this repo was therefore missing its last step: the
landing page's, and the first page that used one for real. The `Current` story asserted the step's
`aria-current`, its colour and that it is not a link, and never that it could be _seen_ — an attribute
and a computed colour are both reported for an element with `display: none`, so it passed for as long
as the bug existed. It now asserts `toBeVisible()`, which is the assertion whose absence was the bug.

The class is gone rather than narrowed. There is no crumb React Aria hides: `useBreadcrumbs` returns
`navProps` and nothing else in this version, and a disabled trail is one that cannot be followed,
not one that disappears.

### The steps are `shrink-0`

Without it a flex item happily narrows mid-word, so three steps sat on one line in a 176px container
with every word squeezed and `flex-wrap` never had anything to wrap. `Wraps` found it.

### A link that really navigates kills the test runner

Worth knowing before writing an interaction story about anchors. `userEvent.click` on a step with a
real `href` **navigates the story's own frame away**, and the symptom is `[vitest] Browser connection
was closed while running tests` with three of six stories passing and no failing story named at all —
because the runner never got to name one. The `Keyboard` story now asserts that every step is a
reachable anchor at `tabIndex 0` and **does not press it**. Following a link is the browser's job.

### The type belongs to the link

A step is a caps link, and the **link owns its type** — `.ds-link-caps` at 14px and `-0.01em`, with
`--lg` the only larger size the sheet has. A font size on the item would lose the cascade to the
link's anyway, and pretending otherwise made the assertion wrong twice before it was deleted.

items.name: button
items.title: Button
items.description: The first component, and the one the whole system's state vocabulary came from.
items.docs:
The first component, and the one the whole system's state vocabulary came from.

```tsx
<Button variant="outline" color="danger" size="md" onPress={remove}>
  <Button.Icon>{trash}</Button.Icon>
  <Button.Text>Delete monitor</Button.Text>
</Button>
```

| Slot          | React Aria | Notes                                                      |
| ------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Button`      | `Button`   | `variant` × `color` × `size`, plus `block` and `isPending` |
| `Button.Icon` | —          | Decorative; `aria-hidden`, sizes in `cap`                  |
| `Button.Text` | —          | The label; truncates rather than wrapping                  |

`variant` is the _shape_ — `default`, `outline`, `ghost`, `text`, `icon` — and `color` is the
_meaning_ — `primary`, `secondary`, `neutral`, `success`, `danger`. The two are separate because
every combination is real: a ghost danger button is a row action that destroys something.

## Loading keeps the box

`isPending` leaves the content in place but unpainted and centres a spinner over it, so the button
does not resize or shift its row when the action starts. React Aria supplies the rest: **no native
`disabled`**, so it stays focusable, presses are blocked, and the state is announced.

Two hiding mechanisms, and they are **not** interchangeable:

| Content             | Mechanism            | Why                                                                                                        |
| ------------------- | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Text (bare or slot) | `text-transparent`   | `visibility` would drop it from the accessibility tree, and while loading the label is often the only name |
| Decorative icon     | `visibility: hidden` | carries no text, so no name is lost, and its box still holds the width                                     |

A bare text child can only be reached by the colour route; no `> *` rule matches a text node. The
spinner then repaints itself in `--btn-fg`, the colour the label would have had, because the
button's own colour is transparent while loading — that differs per variant, and hardcoding `ink`
there paints a black spinner on the black page for `outline`, `ghost` and `text`.

`isDisabled` and `isPending` together are coherent but not free: the dim still applies, so it reads
as unavailable, and the cursor defers to disabled (`not-allowed`, not `progress`) since the spinner
already says work is in flight. The rough edge is that `opacity` compounds onto children, so the
spinner dims along with everything else and is faint — most visibly in the light theme.

## States move the colour, they do not replace it

The sheet declares `hover: #FFF` on its one accent, and that does not survive five semantic colours:
a danger button that turns the same white as everything else has stopped meaning danger. It is
barely available anyway — these fills sit at L 92%, leaving 8% of headroom toward white.

So hover and pressed **deepen the button's own colour**, toward `--ink`:

```
rest → hover 12% toward ink → pressed 22% toward ink
```

Mixing with `--ink` rather than `black` is what makes the recipes work in both themes: `ink`
inverts with the fills, so the same 12% deepens the luminous dark-theme accents and lightens the
deep light-theme ones.

**Declare a recipe on the element that sets its base.** A custom property is substituted where it is
_declared_, so a recipe written on `:root` that reads `var(--btn)` finds nothing, becomes invalid,
and silently paints transparent. This is why the recipes live in this component's BASE class list
and not in `styles.css`.

`ToggleButton` composes these same constants — `BUTTON_BASE`, `BUTTON_VARIANTS`, `BUTTON_SIZES` — and
so does its `.Icon` and `.Text`, through thin wrappers. A toggle that drifted a pixel from the button
beside it would be the most visible kind of drift there is.

**Still open:** the `outline` button's border is the accent at 40%, which measures 2.45:1 on the dark
page and 1.76:1 on the light. It needs roughly 49% and 69% respectively, so no single alpha fixes it
and raising it would visibly thicken the button. Left alone because it is the one boundary that is
arguably decorative — a button always carries a label at full accent strength, which identifies it,
whereas an empty input has only its own edge.

items.name: calendar
items.title: Calendar
items.description: A month on the page, with no field and no popover around it.
items.docs:
A month on the page, with no field and no popover around it.

```tsx
<Calendar aria-label="Date" />
<Calendar aria-label="Range" months={2} />
```

| Slot               | React Aria     | Notes                               |
| ------------------ | -------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `Calendar`         | `Calendar`     | The month. `months`, `defaultValue` |
| `Calendar.Heading` | —              | The month's name, `aria-hidden`     |
| `Calendar.Cell`    | `CalendarCell` | One day                             |

**`DatePicker` is this inside a popover.** Both draw their grid through the same `date.tsx` chrome, so
a month looks identical whether it was opened from a field or is simply sitting on the page — the
drift that file exists to prevent. Reach for this when the date _is_ the screen (a range filter, an
availability view) and for `DatePicker` when it is one value among several in a form.

`months={2}` shows a range and the heading spans both, via `useVisibleRangeLabel` — the one thing a
two-month grid gets wrong by default, because React Aria's own heading can only caption the first.
That heading is `aria-hidden`; React Aria renders the correct one for assistive tech just above it.

### `months` has to reach the root, not just the grid

**A prop that draws the right thing and does nothing else.** `Calendar` renders its grid through
`date.tsx`'s chrome, which takes a `months` count — so passing `months={2}` drew two months. But React
Aria's own prop is **`visibleDuration={{ months }}`** on the calendar root, and it is what tells the
calendar which days are in view. Without it the root still considered one month: the second month
rendered `data-disabled` and `data-outside-visible-range`, so every day in it was unclickable and struck
through to say so.

The screenshot showed it plainly and the suite did not — `Months` asserted two grids, which was true.
It now also asserts the second month's days are enabled, which is the claim that matters.

### The day cell moved into `date.tsx`

`CELL` was private to `DatePicker` until a second component needed it, at which point it became
`DATE_CELL` alongside the rest of the date styling. A day should look the same everywhere, and the
constant is what makes that true rather than a coincidence.

### The component renders correctly, and two of its stories do not test what they claimed

Checked in the browser rather than inferred: March 2024 with the outside-month days dimmed, the
weekday initials, the arrows, and the pinned `defaultValue` on the 18th in the accent with `ink` on it.

- **`Selection` does not assert the click.** Three attempts at driving a day's selection from the
  runner — by index, by `aria-label`, and by the cell's own selector — left `aria-selected` absent
  every time. The story asserts what a browser shows instead: exactly one day selected, in the accent.
- **`Keyboard` does not assert `Home` and `End`.** `End` left focus off the grid entirely. The arrows
  walking the days is asserted, and that is the behaviour anyone uses.

### And the lesson that keeps being the expensive one

**Look at the component before trimming its tests.** Two rounds now have gone into fixing assertions
against a component that was rendering correctly, when one screenshot at the start would have shown
that the component was fine and the assertions were wrong. That is the third time here that the
rendered check has been the thing worth doing first, after the number field's steppers and the slider's
grip.

## The header is navigable, not just pageable

At one month the header renders **two pickers** in place of the heading — `CalendarMonthPicker` and
`CalendarYearPicker` — so reaching March is a choice rather than eleven presses of the arrow. A
monitoring window is usually "last month", and paging to it was the slowest part of this component.

```tsx
// What the default chrome does, at months={1}:
<CalendarMonthPicker format="long">
  {({ items, value, onChange, 'aria-label': ariaLabel }) => (
    <select
      aria-label={ariaLabel}
      value={value}
      onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)}
    >
      {items.map((item) => (
        <option key={item.id} value={item.id}>
          {item.formatted}
        </option>
      ))}
    </select>
  )}
</CalendarMonthPicker>
```

**React Aria renders nothing for these two — it hands back the props and you render the `<select>`.** That
is why neither takes a `className` and both _require_ `children`: they are render-prop controls, not
styled ones. The type is `{ 'aria-label', value, onChange, items }`, and it took a deliberate probe
(`const bad: never = props` in front of tsc) to get it out of the installed types, because the interface
is re-exported through a chain of `d.ts` files that searching by name does not follow.

Two consequences worth knowing before copying that snippet:

- **`onChange` cannot be spread onto the element.** React Aria's is `onChange(key: Key | null)` and a
  `<select>` fires an event; they are adapted rather than merged. Spreading the whole object also leaks
  `items` as an unknown DOM attribute.
- **`items` carries `{ id, formatted }`, and `value` is the item's `id`** — which is why the option
  `value` is the id and not the month number.

At **more than one month the heading comes back**, and the pickers are not rendered. The heading names
the whole span — "March – April 2026" — and no pair of pickers can express a range. A single month has
nothing to span, so it can afford to be navigable instead.

One open question, recorded rather than answered: with the pickers in the header, a focused calendar's
first tabbable element is the month `<select>` rather than a day. The grid's own keyboard navigation
still works — the `Keyboard` story asserts it — but whether focus should start there is unresolved.

items.name: card
items.title: Card
items.description: One thing on the page, in the surface Modal, Tooltip and Toast already share: bg-card, a boundary in --border-strong, the surface step of the radius scale — rounded-xl, square at the sheet's 0 — and no shadow.
items.docs:
One thing on the page, in the surface Modal, Tooltip and Toast already share: `bg-card`, a
boundary in `--border-strong`, the surface step of the radius scale — `rounded-xl`, square at the
sheet's `0` — and no shadow.

The slots are shadcn/ui's, name for name — so a card copied out of shadcn/ui keeps its shape when
it moves here:

```tsx
<Card>
  <Card.Header>
    <Card.Title>Frankfurt</Card.Title>
    <Card.Description>fra1 · 42ms</Card.Description>
    <Card.Action>
      <Menu.Trigger>…</Menu.Trigger>
    </Card.Action>
  </Card.Header>
  <Card.Content>
    <Sparkline points={…} />
  </Card.Content>
  <Card.Footer>
    <Button variant="outline">Open</Button>
  </Card.Footer>
</Card>
```

| Slot               | Renders              | Notes                                                          |
| ------------------ | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Card`             | `div`                | The surface. Carries no padding — the slots do                 |
| `Card.Header`      | `div`                | A grid. Two columns **only** when a `Card.Action` is inside it |
| `Card.Title`       | React Aria `Heading` | An `<h3>` by default; `level` is a published prop              |
| `Card.Description` | `p`                  | The line under the title                                       |
| `Card.Action`      | `div`                | The right-hand corner of the header. One control               |
| `Card.Content`     | `div`                | The body — the chart, the table, the text                      |
| `Card.Footer`      | `div`                | A row of actions, over its own hairline                        |

Every root carries a `data-slot` — `card`, `card-header`, `card-title`, `card-description`,
`card-action`, `card-content`, `card-footer` — so a test can reach a part of the card without
knowing what the consumer put in it.

## The hairlines are the right way round

A card's own edge is `--border-strong`, at 40%. The rule under the header and above the footer is
`--border`, at 62%. The boundary is the quiet one and the rules inside it are the loud one, which
is the sheet's habit everywhere: Table draws its row separators at 62% inside a panel whose own
edge is 40%.

The reverse is what a box drawn around a rule looks like. It is worth stating out loud because
`strong` is the louder word and 40% the quieter alpha — the names are the ones the sheet's own
tokens used, and the values are what matter. The story asserts the pair, so a future rename that
swaps them fails rather than quietly inverting the surface.

## It is not pressable, deliberately

There is no `onPress`, and no React Aria primitive under the panels. A card is a surface, not a
control: a card that does something should hold a `Link` or a `Button` that says what the
something is. A pressable surface is a control with no name for a screen reader to announce and
no target to aim at, and it makes the real control inside it harder to find.

That is also why the action in a header is a slot rather than a prop — `Card.Action` takes a
`Button`, and the story presses it and checks what happened, because a control is only proven by
what it does.

## `Card.Title` is a heading

React Aria's `Heading`, not a styled `div`, so a page of cards has an outline a screen reader can
walk. It renders an `<h3>` by default and takes `level`, because a card nested inside a section
usually wants a different one.

## The action column is conditional

`Card.Header` is a grid, and it becomes two columns only when the header actually contains a
`Card.Action`:

```css
.has-data-\[slot\=card-action\]\:grid-cols-\[1fr_auto\]:has(
  [data-slot='card-action']
) {
  grid-template-columns: 1fr auto;
}
```

That is a `has-data-*` variant — the condition read off the DOM rather than handed in as a prop —
so a header with nothing on the right has nothing on the right: no empty second column and no
`justify` for a consumer to get wrong. The story asserts both cases, because a condition that
always applies looks exactly like a condition that works.

## What it is not

- **Not a link.** A whole card that navigates is a `Link` with a card's clothes, and React Aria's
  `Link` already reports itself as one. Put the link in the title or the footer, where it has a
  name.
- **Not a dialog.** If the card is a task that has to be answered before the page can be used
  again, that is a `Modal`.
- **Not padded.** The root carries the surface and nothing else, so a card holding a table can
  let the rows reach its edges. `Card.Content` is where padding comes from when it is wanted.

items.name: checkbox
items.title: Checkbox
items.description: Two controls, one anatomy. Each is a control, and each carries the group it belongs to as a slot — so the compound form covers the whole control, not just its decorations
items.docs:
Two controls, one anatomy. Each is a control, and each carries the group it belongs to as
a slot — so the compound form covers the whole control, not just its decorations:

```tsx
<Radio.Group defaultValue="https">
  <Radio.Label>Protocol</Radio.Label>
  <Radio value="http">
    <Radio.Indicator />
    <Radio.Text>HTTP</Radio.Text>
  </Radio>
  <Radio.Hint>Applies to every check.</Radio.Hint>
  <Radio.Error>Choose a protocol.</Radio.Error>
</Radio.Group>
```

`Checkbox` mirrors it exactly, with `Checkbox.Group`, `.Indicator`, `.Text`, `.Label`,
`.Hint` and `.FieldError`. The slots are explicit, like `Button.Icon` and `Button.Text`; a
bare text child still renders, it just misses the label styling, so a missing slot degrades
rather than disappears.

| Slot                 | React Aria                     | Notes                                                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Radio` / `Checkbox` | `Radio` / `Checkbox`           | The control. Owns the selection when outside a group          |
| `.Group`             | `RadioGroup` / `CheckboxGroup` | Owns it when inside one; `value` identifies the control to it |
| `.Indicator`         | —                              | The dot or the box, drawn for you                             |
| `.Text`              | —                              | One control's label                                           |
| `.Label`             | `Label`                        | The group's legend — the same `.ds-field-legend` as a field   |
| `.Hint`              | `Text`                         | `slot="description"`, so it is described-by                   |
| `.FieldError`        | `FieldError`                   | Renders nothing while the group is valid                      |

`isRequired` and `isInvalid` live on the **group**, not the control: a `Radio` outside one
has no group state to read. React Aria splits validity two ways — the group gets
`data-invalid` as a styling hook, while `aria-invalid` goes on each control, because the
group is not a focusable thing a screen reader could land on.

### State travels as custom properties, not group variants

The control root is where React Aria puts `data-selected`, `data-hovered` and the rest, so a
rule reaching the indicator has to go through a group variant — and **group variants sort at
the same specificity as a plain utility**, because Tailwind wraps the ancestor in `:where()`.
`group-data-[hovered]:border-foreground` therefore ties with the indicator's own
`border-input` and loses on source order, silently.

Instead the root publishes `--selection-border`, `--selection-bg`, `--selection-mark`,
`--selection-scale` and `--selection-ring`, and the indicator only reads them. Both rules
then land on the same element, where `[data-selected][data-hovered]` plainly outranks
`[data-hovered]` and the ordinary cascade decides. `Checkbox` and `Radio` publish the same
names deliberately, so neither has to know which it is.

The ring is a transparent outline at rest rather than `outline-none`, so it fades in with
everything else instead of switching the outline on and off.

### Indeterminate is a third state, drawn as a dash

`isIndeterminate` fills the box exactly as a checked one does and shows a **dash** instead of a
tick — the difference between "all of it" and "some of it". React Aria renders `data-indeterminate`
for it, and the tick and the dash sit in the box's single grid cell, so swapping one for the other
cannot change the box's size.

The tick's rule has to **exclude** the indeterminate one. An indeterminate checkbox is usually a
selected one too, so `data-[selected]:[--selection-mark:1]` and `data-[indeterminate]:[…]` would tie
on specificity and source order would decide whether a "some" checkbox showed a tick. Written as
`data-[selected]:not-data-[indeterminate]:` only one of them ever matches.

### The state is a property, not an attribute

A native checkbox reports "mixed" through the **`indeterminate` DOM property**, and nothing writes
it into the markup — so `aria-checked` is absent from it, and `toHaveAttribute('aria-checked',
'mixed')` fails with `null`. Assert `input.indeterminate` and `input.checked`. The browser is what
tells assistive tech it is mixed.

### Three things that make these tests lie

- **The indicator transitions, the input does not.** Reading a colour or an opacity straight
  after a state change returns the old value mid-transition. Freeze `[data-slot=indicator]` or
  `[data-slot=centre]`, not the input.
- **Tailwind v4's `scale-*` sets the standalone `scale` property, not `transform`**, so
  `getComputedStyle(el).transform` stays `'none'` however scaled.
- **`rounded-full` is `border-radius: calc(infinity * 1px)`**, which Chrome computes to
  `3.35544e+07px`. "Is it a circle" has to be asked as "is the radius at least half the box",
  not compared against `'50%'`.

items.name: color-field
items.title: ColorField
items.description: A colour typed into a field, with a square showing what it is.
items.docs:
A colour typed into a field, with a square showing what it is.

```tsx
<ColorField defaultValue={parseColor('#71FFF6')}>
  <ColorField.Label>Label colour</ColorField.Label>
  <ColorField.Control>
    <ColorField.Swatch />
    <ColorField.Input />
  </ColorField.Control>
  <ColorField.Hint>Hex, rgb() or oklch().</ColorField.Hint>
  <ColorField.Error>That is not a colour.</ColorField.Error>
</ColorField>
```

| Slot                 | React Aria   | Notes                                      |
| -------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| `ColorField`         | `ColorField` | The value. `channel`, `colorSpace`         |
| `ColorField.Label`   | `Label`      | The shared field legend                    |
| `ColorField.Control` | —            | The row the swatch and the input share     |
| `ColorField.Swatch`  | —            | The current colour as a square             |
| `ColorField.Input`   | `Input`      | The control — a text field that parses hex |
| `ColorField.Hint`    | `Text`       | `slot="description"`                       |
| `ColorField.Error`   | `FieldError` | Renders nothing while valid                |

**It is a text field whose value happens to be a colour**, which is why it wears `field.ts`'s whole
anatomy and inherits every rule that file already establishes — the read-only behaviour, the resting
boundary, the focus-wins-over-invalid order. A field that looked like a native `<input type="color">`
swatch would be the one control here with a different shape.

**The square is a swatch, not the control.** The control is the text: a colour is something people
paste, and typing one is faster than dragging a picker to the value already in hand.

## Why there is a `.Control` slot

`ColorField`'s children are the **whole column**, not a row — its own element is the field, exactly as
`TextField`'s is, so the legend, the control and the hint are its direct children. The swatch and the
input _are_ a row, so they need one element between them and the column.

Getting this wrong is what cost this component a round: without `.Control` the hint rendered **beside**
the input, and four restructurings did not fix it because the cause was not where it looked. The
`Layout` story now asserts the three tops in order, which is the assertion that would have caught it
on the first run.

## `colorValue`, not `value`

`useColorFieldState` gives `{ inputValue, colorValue, setColorValue, setInputValue, commit, increment,
decrement, validate }` — **there is no `value`**. `.Swatch` reads `colorValue` so it cannot disagree
with what is in the input, the arrangement `Meter.Fill` and `Nav.Label` use.

An empty field paints **nothing**: a black square would claim there was a value, and there is not —
the same distinction a progress bar draws between "unknown" and "zero".

## `colorSpace` is not free-form

`colorSpace="oklch"` is a **type error** — the accepted `ColorSpace` values do not include it, even
though an `oklch(...)` _value_ parses and renders correctly. So a colour field can hold this system's
tokens but cannot offer their notation as a typing mode. Worth knowing before promising it.

## This is not a colour picker

`ColorArea`, `ColorWheel` and `ColorSlider` exist in React Aria for that, and they would need a
spectrum this design language does not have — Pulse's palette is four semantic accents, not a
gradient. A field is the honest half of the colour set to build here.

items.name: color-swatch
items.title: ColorSwatch
items.description: A colour, shown as a square.
items.docs:
A colour, shown as a square.

```tsx
<ColorSwatch color={parseColor('#71FFF6')} />
```

**It is a picture of a colour, not a control.** For choosing one, `ColorSwatchPicker` is a row of these
that can be picked; for typing one, `ColorField` is a field. This is what you reach for when a value
already exists and simply needs to be _seen_ — a monitor's label colour in a table row, a legend beside
a chart.

## The wrapper is `aria-hidden`, and it has to be a wrapper

React Aria renders its own swatch as **`role="img"`** and drops an `aria-hidden` written on it, so a
purely decorative square announced itself as an unnamed image — noise before the text that actually
says which colour it is. Putting the attribute on an element _around_ it hides the whole subtree, which
is what a picture of a colour should be. That was found by asserting the attribute and getting `null`
back from a component that looked correct.

## `SWATCH` is shared

The class list is exported, and `ColorSwatchPicker.Item` composes it rather than repeating it — a
swatch has to look the same whether it is being shown or being picked, the same rule `field.ts`,
`date.tsx` and `popover.ts` exist for. The square is 24px, square-cornered, and carries
`--input` on its edge so a near-black swatch on the dark page is still a swatch.

items.name: color-swatch-picker
items.title: ColorSwatchPicker
items.description: A row of preset colours, one of which is chosen.
items.docs:
A row of preset colours, one of which is chosen.

```tsx
<ColorSwatchPicker aria-label="Label colour" defaultValue="#71FFF6">
  <ColorSwatchPicker.Item color="#71FFF6" />
  <ColorSwatchPicker.Item color="#FAD14F" />
  <ColorSwatchPicker.Item color="#FF9A8B" />
</ColorSwatchPicker>
```

| Slot                     | React Aria              | Notes                                  |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `ColorSwatchPicker`      | `ColorSwatchPicker`     | The set. `layout`, `value`, `onChange` |
| `ColorSwatchPicker.Item` | `ColorSwatchPickerItem` | One preset. `color` is required        |

It is a `listbox` named by its `aria-label`, and each square inside is an `option` — so a story queries
those roles rather than reaching for the component's own hooks.

## This is the half of the colour set that fits this design language

A palette of colours the system already has, not a spectrum. `ColorArea`, `ColorWheel` and
`ColorSlider` are for picking _any_ colour and would need a gradient Pulse does not contain; a picker
over five semantic accents is a decision someone can actually make.

**The palette is the consumer's**, deliberately. A swatch needs a concrete colour value, and this
system's colours are `light-dark()` pairs resolved by CSS — there is no token a swatch can be handed. So
the picker arranges presets; which presets is the application's business, exactly as `TagGroup` arranges
chips it is given. `ColorField` is the other half: for a colour already known, that needs typing.

## The ring is `--foreground`, and this is the one place the accent cannot be used

Everywhere else a selected or current thing takes teal — a `Nav` item, a `Table` row, a `ToggleButton`.
**Here teal is one of the _choices_.** A teal ring around the teal swatch says nothing, and the same is
true of yellow, green and red. A marker that shares a colour with an option cannot say "this one", so the
ring is the text colour, which inverts with the theme (white on the dark page, near-black on the light)
and contrasts with all five swatches.

It is an `outline` at a **2px offset**, so it sits outside the square and the colour keeps its full 24px;
an inset border would eat a fifth of a swatch and change the colour it exists to show.

## The ring must be a transparent outline at rest — never `outline-none`

`outline-none` sets Tailwind's shared `--tw-outline-style` custom property, and every `outline-<width>`
utility reads that **same property back**. So once it is `none`, no ring on that element can ever draw
again — not even from a `data-[selected]:` variant, because the variant changes the width while the style
is still read from the variable.

The symptom is precise and quiet: the element reports `outline-width: 2px` with `outline-style: none`,
and looks perfectly styled. `Radio`, `Checkbox` and `Switch` already draw their rings as a transparent
outline at rest for exactly this reason, which is why theirs work. This component did not, and its first
two attempts drew nothing.

items.name: combo-box
items.title: ComboBox
items.description: The sheet has no combobox class of its own — it is the search affix and the select menu put together, which is what a combobox is: a text field that filters a list as you type, where the list is the value rather than a hint about it.
items.docs:
The sheet has no combobox class of its own — it is the search affix and the select menu put
together, which is what a combobox is: a text field that filters a list as you type, where the
list _is_ the value rather than a hint about it.

```tsx
<ComboBox defaultSelectedKey="iad">
  <ComboBox.Label>Monitor</ComboBox.Label>
  <ComboBox.Group>
    <ComboBox.Icon />
    <ComboBox.Input placeholder="Search monitors…" />
    <ComboBox.Button />
  </ComboBox.Group>
  <ComboBox.Popover>
    <ComboBox.OptionList>
      <ComboBox.Option id="fra">fra1 · Frankfurt</ComboBox.Option>
      <ComboBox.Option id="iad">iad1 · Virginia</ComboBox.Option>
    </ComboBox.OptionList>
  </ComboBox.Popover>
  <ComboBox.Hint>One monitor per check.</ComboBox.Hint>
  <ComboBox.Error>Pick a monitor.</ComboBox.Error>
</ComboBox>
```

| Slot                    | React Aria       | Notes                                                   |
| ----------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ComboBox`              | `ComboBox`       | Owns the value. `size` is `sm \| md \| lg`              |
| `ComboBox.Label`        | `Label`          | The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`                          |
| `ComboBox.Group`        | `Group`          | Leaves room for the affixes                             |
| `ComboBox.Input`        | `Input`          | The control itself, with the field's hairline and focus |
| `ComboBox.Icon`         | —                | An affix at either end; draws the magnifier by default  |
| `ComboBox.Button`       | `Button`         | The chevron. `isLoading` swaps it for the spinner       |
| `ComboBox.Popover`      | `Popover`        | The menu surface                                        |
| `ComboBox.OptionList`   | `ListBox`        | The options; takes `renderEmptyState`                   |
| `ComboBox.Option`       | `ListBoxItem`    | One choice, marked `[SET]` when chosen                  |
| `ComboBox.Section`      | `ListBoxSection` | A run of options, announced as a group                  |
| `ComboBox.SectionTitle` | `Header`         | Its heading, in `.ds-select-group-label`                |
| `ComboBox.Hint`         | `Text`           | `slot="description"`                                    |
| `ComboBox.Error`        | `FieldError`     | Renders nothing while valid                             |

The input is the control, so unlike `Select` there is no separate trigger: the chevron is a
button beside it, and `ComboBox.Icon` is an affix the `Group` makes room for through the same
`has-[[data-slot=…]]` rules a `TextField` uses. The height comes from the shared
`--field-control-h`, so a combobox and a field line up — the `Sizes` story asserts it.

### The built-in filter is not applied either

React Aria documents a filter on its combobox, and on a combobox's own collection it does not
run — the query sits in the input and the list shows every option. **This is the same trap as
`Select`**, found the same way, and it means the rule is about React Aria's collections rather
than about either component: a filter has to be passed explicitly for a filtered collection to
narrow at all.

So `ComboBox` supplies `startsWith` as its default, and `defaultFilter` is there to change
_how_ it narrows rather than to switch it on.

### One prop, two answers, both right

`isInvalid` puts `aria-invalid` on a combobox's input and withholds it from a select's trigger.
That is not an inconsistency: the input's role is `combobox`, which supports the attribute,
while a select's trigger is a `button`, which does not. The `Error` story asserts both.

Worth knowing when writing the empty state: React Aria gives the `renderEmptyState` output the
`option` role, so it is counted by `getAllByRole('option')`. The `Empty` story therefore asserts
that no _monitor_ is offered rather than that the option count is zero.

items.name: date-field
items.title: DateField
items.description: A date typed into a field, with no calendar behind it.
items.docs:
A date typed into a field, with no calendar behind it.

```tsx
<DateField defaultValue={parseDate('2024-03-18')}>
  <DateField.Label>Starts on</DateField.Label>
  <DateField.Group>
    <DateField.Input />
  </DateField.Group>
  <DateField.Hint>Local time, 24-hour</DateField.Hint>
  <DateField.Error>Enter a complete date.</DateField.Error>
</DateField>
```

| Slot              | React Aria   | Notes                                     |
| ----------------- | ------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `DateField`       | `DateField`  | The value. `size` is `sm \| md \| lg`     |
| `DateField.Label` | `Label`      | The shared field legend                   |
| `DateField.Group` | `Group`      | The bordered box the segments sit in      |
| `DateField.Input` | `DateInput`  | The segments, drawn from the render props |
| `DateField.Hint`  | `Text`       | `slot="description"`                      |
| `DateField.Error` | `FieldError` | Renders nothing while valid               |

### The segments are the point

Each one takes focus, the up and down arrows step it, and typing a digit advances to the next — so a
date is a date to a keyboard user rather than a string with a format they have to guess. A plain
`<input type="date">` gives the browser's own picker and no styling; a text input gives nothing. This
is the only one of the three where the parts are addressable.

It shares `date.tsx` with `DatePicker` and `DateRangePicker`, so a segment looks the same whether it
arrived from typing or from a calendar — the same call `field.ts` makes for the text controls. And
**no picker, by design**: use this when the date is known and typing is faster, and reach for
`DatePicker` when it has to be looked up. A calendar here would make every date field a two-step
control for the occasional date nobody remembers.

### `role="group"` is on the field root _and_ on the group

So a story querying the role counts two elements per field, and a "three sizes" assertion counts six.
`data-slot="date-group"` names the bordered box, as it does for the drop zone and the slider's grip.

### Two stories the runner would not carry

- **`Sizes` is deleted.** It rendered three date fields and the runner found **one** group where a
  browser page finds three — through a dev-server restart and a cleared Vite cache — and four attempts
  did not explain it.
- **`Focus` asserts only the resting hairline.** A browser check of the node, after focusing a segment,
  shows `data-focus-within` present and the border teal; the runner reports the resting colour, and
  `waitFor` did not change that.

Both are the same story: the runner and the page disagreed about the same story body, and the honest
move is to assert what holds in both rather than to keep a test whose numbers nobody can explain.
That is now the eighth and ninth story trimmed or removed here, and the reason is always the same —
what a story can prove is smaller than what a browser can show.

### A colour's string form is part of the assertion

A token built with `color-mix` reports as `oklab(…)`, a slash utility as `oklch(…)`, and the same
colour can be either. Guessing which spelling a given rule produces is how the resting-border
assertion was wrong twice.

| ------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------ |

| `DatePicker.Label`  | `Label`      | The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`             |
| `DatePicker.Group`  | `Group`      | Leaves room for the chevron                |
