| `DatePicker.Button` | `Button`     | The chevron                                |
| `DatePicker.Hint`   | `Text`       | `slot="description"`                       |
| `DatePicker.Error`  | `FieldError` | Renders nothing while valid                |

### The calendar is drawn for you

A picker without a calendar is not a picker, so `DatePicker` renders the popover and the whole
month itself and the field is the entire API. **The calendar is not replaceable** — the popover and the
month it opens are internal, so unlike `Select.Popover` there is nothing to pass in its place.

The reason is the same one that shaped `Select.AutoComplete`: React Aria builds a calendar from a
grid, a header, a body and two render props — six elements before a single day appears — and not
one of those is a decision the consumer is making. The calendar's own parts are internal for the same
reason: a slot that exists only so it can be taken apart publishes a surface nobody uses, and the `Pieces`
story that exercised it has been removed with them.

### The value is a `DateValue`, not a string

`defaultValue={parseDate('2026-10-11')}` and `onChange` hands back the same shape. That is what
keeps the field locale-aware: the segments, the month name and the order they appear in all
follow the locale rather than a format the code chose.

### What the calendar had to decide

Three states that are easy to collapse into one, and should not be:

| State                        | Treatment                              |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| outside the month            | dimmed                                 |
| today                        | outlined in the accent, **not** filled |
| out of `minValue`/`maxValue` | dimmed _and_ struck through            |
| chosen                       | filled with the accent, carrying `ink` |

Leaving today looking exactly like every other day is the usual way a calendar makes someone
ask what today is. Out-of-range days stay in the grid rather than being removed — a month with
holes in it is much harder to read than one where the gaps are marked. And the chosen day is the
same pair the sheet uses for a checked box: an accent fill with `ink` on it.

A focused segment is **not** given that fill. A field's focus is a teal _border_ here, so filling
a segment in the accent would say "chosen" about a segment that is only being typed; it gets the
same faint wash the sheet puts behind a hovered option.

### Four things this cost, all worth writing down

- **`data-unavailable` and `data-disabled` are different attributes.** A day outside
  `minValue`/`maxValue` is `unavailable`; a day in a wholly disabled calendar is `disabled`. Both
  need the treatment, and styling only one leaves the other looking perfectly selectable.
- **The strike-through is on the cell, not on the button inside it.** The inner `role=button`
  reports `text-decoration: none` of its own, so asking it whether the day is struck out always
  says no. The cell carries `data-slot="cell"` so the test can address the right box.
- **React Aria renders the month heading twice** — once for the accessibility tree and once for
  the eye — so `getByText(/october 2026/)` finds two and fails. Ask for it by role: the duplicate
  is `aria-hidden`, so a role query sees one.
- **A story named `Error` shadows the global.** `new Error(…)` inside `DatePicker.stories.tsx`
  resolves to the story export, and TypeScript reports it as "not constructable" rather than as
  a name collision. Assert with `toBeInstanceOf` instead.

React Aria names the calendar button itself — "Calendar", from the field's context — so there is
nothing to pass and nothing to drift. `getByRole('button')` alone, then assert the name, rather
than matching on a string we did not write.

items.name: date-range-picker
items.title: DateRangePicker
items.description: Two dates as one value — "when does this window start and end". The difference from two DatePickers is not cosmetic: a range has a validity of its own (the end cannot precede the start), one calendar serves both ends, and the days between are shown as chosen rather than as two unrelated picks.
items.docs:
Two dates as one value — "when does this window start and end". The difference from two
`DatePicker`s is not cosmetic: a range has a validity of its own (the end cannot precede the
start), one calendar serves both ends, and the days between are shown as chosen rather than as
two unrelated picks.

```tsx
<DateRangePicker
  defaultValue={{
    start: parseDate('2026-10-11'),
    end: parseDate('2026-10-20'),
  }}
>
  <DateRangePicker.Label>Window</DateRangePicker.Label>
  <DateRangePicker.Group>
    <DateRangePicker.Input />
    <DateRangePicker.Button />
  </DateRangePicker.Group>
  <DateRangePicker.Hint>Your local time.</DateRangePicker.Hint>
</DateRangePicker>
```

| Slot                     | React Aria        | Notes                                      |
| ------------------------ | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `DateRangePicker`        | `DateRangePicker` | Owns the range. `size` is `sm \| md \| lg` |
| `DateRangePicker.Label`  | `Label`           | The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`             |
| `DateRangePicker.Group`  | `Group`           | Leaves room for the chevron                |
| `DateRangePicker.Input`  | two `DateInput`s  | Both ends _and_ the separator, in one slot |
| `DateRangePicker.Button` | `Button`          | The chevron                                |
| `DateRangePicker.Hint`   | `Text`            | `slot="description"`                       |
| `DateRangePicker.Error`  | `FieldError`      | Renders nothing while valid                |

### One slot for both ends

`DateRangePicker.Input` draws the start input, the separator and the end input. React Aria needs
to be told which is which (`slot="start"` / `slot="end"`), and a consumer writing that by hand can
get it backwards in a way that still renders. Drawing it here also means the field's hairline is
drawn **once around both**, rather than twice with a seam down the middle — the two inputs share
one control, so `DateRangePicker.Input` is a `<div>` carrying the field's shape and the state
that lands on it comes from the root.

Because of that, its props are deliberately narrower than a `DateInput`'s: this is two inputs and
one control, so input-level props have no single input to go to.

### The shared anatomy, and the one part that is not

`src/components/date.tsx` holds everything the two date components do not differ on — the field
root, the caret, the trigger, the menu surface, the segment, the month's arrows, its heading, the
weekday row and the whole calendar chrome — the same split as `field.ts`. The slots are still
defined per component, so Storybook documents `DatePicker.Label` as `DatePicker.Label` rather
than as its neighbour's.

The one part that genuinely differs is the day. In a range **every day between the ends is
selected**, so the ends have to be told apart from the middle: the ends carry the accent whole,
the days between take it as a wash. Without that, a range reads as two separate picks that happen
to be far apart.

### Three rules that cannot both match

The obvious way to write that is an endpoint rule that out-specifies the wash. Both of the
obvious ways fail, and both fail silently:

- **Stacking two data variants does not compile.** `data-[selected][data-selection-start]:bg-primary`
  emits nothing at all — the selector never appears in the stylesheet, so the ends simply keep
  the wash and the day looks like every other day in the range.
- **A single `data-[selection-start]` ties with `data-[selected]`** — both are one variant — and
  loses on source order.

So the three rules are written to be **mutually exclusive** instead, and only ever one applies:

```
data-[selection-start]:bg-primary          the ends, whole
data-[selection-end]:bg-primary
data-[selected]:not-data-[selection-start]:not-data-[selection-end]:bg-primary/20   the middle, washed
```

### The chrome draws one grid per month

A multi-month calendar needs **one `CalendarGrid` per month, each with its own `offset`**. With a
single grid, `visibleDuration={{ months: 2 }}` renders a heading spanning both months above a grid
showing only the first — the heading promising something the grid does not deliver, which is
worse than not offering the prop. `DateCalendarChrome` takes `months` and draws that many.

### The states a range cannot put on its own control

`data-invalid` and `data-disabled` land on the picker's **root**, while the control they should
recolour is the `<div>` wrapping both inputs. So the shared root publishes `--field-border` for
invalid and `--date-control-opacity` for disabled, and the control reads them — the same
arrangement `Select` uses for its trigger, and for the same reason.

## Two months, always

The popover opens on **two months**, and it is not configurable:

```tsx
<DateRangePicker
  defaultValue={{
    start: parseDate('2026-10-11'),
    end: parseDate('2026-10-20'),
  }}
>
  <DateRangePicker.Label>Window</DateRangePicker.Label>
  <DateRangePicker.Group>
    <DateRangePicker.Input />
    <DateRangePicker.Button />
  </DateRangePicker.Group>
</DateRangePicker>
```

A range's two ends are rarely in the same month, so one month would make the common case a second
interaction. It was briefly a `visibleDuration` prop, and before that reachable only through a
`DateRangePicker.Calendar` slot; both are gone. The picker decides.

**Both halves have to agree.** React Aria's calendar and the shared `DateCalendarChrome` each need telling —
the calendar draws the heading, the chrome draws the grids. Handing the duration to only the first produces a
heading reading "October to November 2026" above a single grid of October days. A heading assertion passes
straight through that; the `TwoMonths` story asserts a **day in the second month**, which is what catches it.

items.name: dot-map
items.title: DotMap
items.description: A world map drawn as dots, with the ones that matter in the accent.
items.docs:
A world map drawn as dots, with the ones that matter in the accent.

```tsx
import { WORLD_DOTS } from './worldDots'

;<DotMap
  dots={[...WORLD_DOTS, [292.5, 243.5, 1, 'fra1 · 1.2m']]}
  label="Request origins, last hour"
/>
```

| prop             | default | notes                                                    |
| ---------------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dots`           | —       | `[x, y]`, `[x, y, 1]` for the accent, `[x, y, 1, label]` |
| `width`/`height` | 528/380 | user units **and** rendered px                           |
| `fit`            | `true`  | scale and centre the points into the box                 |
| `label`          | —       | required; the drawing's only text                        |

## The drawing is `drawMap`, and there is almost nothing to it

Every point is a `2.6×2.6` **rect** centred on its coordinate, filled either near-white or with a dimmer teal.
The replica fades them in left to right; that is deliberately not copied, because a staggered fade is a
page-level flourish rather than a property of the map.

**Two colours, both derived rather than copied.** The replica writes `#5be4dc` for an accented dot and
`rgba(255,255,255,.85)` for the rest. The first is the accent about 12% toward ink — a small dot at full
accent is a glare, so it is dimmed by the rule every other state here uses. The second is `--foreground` at
85%: white on the dark theme, near-black on the light one, which is the right behaviour for a map on a white
page that the replica never had to consider.

## The fit, and why the data forced it

The dataset's own range is about `x 81–482`, `y 144–401` — 401 tall — while the zone `dashboard.html` gives it
is `528×380`. The comment there says the dots are _"scaled ~0.93 into a 528×380 zone, centered"_, and that
scaling lives in the page, not in `drawMap`. Doing it here means the data and the box can change
independently, which is what makes this a component rather than a snippet. `Unfitted` asserts that the raw
coordinates really do put dots past the bottom edge, so the default is doing work rather than being decorative.

## The readout is opt-in through the data

**The replica's map has no tooltip, and cannot have one.** `GEO_DOTS` is bare geometry with no values, so
there is nothing to say about an individual point — a dot map here answers _where_, not _how much_.

Give a dot a fourth element and it becomes hoverable: the map finds the nearest labelled dot within **10
units** of the pointer and shows its text above it. Unlabelled dots are skipped, so a pointer over the ocean
finds nothing rather than the nearest coastline fragment.

It is `aria-hidden`, the same as the chart's readout: something that exists only under a pointer is not
available to a keyboard, so announcing it would claim an affordance this cannot keep. Where the values matter,
they belong in a `Table` beside the map.

## `WORLD_DOTS` is generated, not hand-written

`src/components/DotMap/worldDots.ts` holds 848 points, 69 of them accented, produced from
`pulse-replica/js/data.js`. It is data rather than design, so it lives in its own module: a consumer that
never draws the map never pays for it.

**Regenerate it with `node scripts/gen-world-dots.mjs`, not by editing the file.** The first version of
this was generated by a throwaway script that was then deleted, which left a derived file with no
derivation — indistinguishable from a hand-written one, and this doc telling a reader to regenerate it when
`data.js` changed, which was not possible. The script reads `GEO_DOTS` out of the replica's plain browser
script with a regex (it is a top-level `const`, not a module), parses the array as the JSON it already is,
and writes the module. Running it twice produces byte-identical output.

## It draws on a `<canvas>`, not an `<svg>`

The replica builds its map by appending ~850 `<rect>` elements into an `<svg>`. This draws the same `2.6`
squares with `fillRect` instead, because 850 DOM nodes for one picture is the cost a canvas exists to avoid —
and it makes the pointer handling cheaper, since hit-testing is already arithmetic against the dot list
rather than a listener per element.

**Canvas costs three things the SVG had for free, and each is handled rather than ignored:**

1. **A canvas cannot read `var()` or `color-mix()`.** `fillStyle` needs a concrete colour. The two fills are
   resolved by assigning the expression to the canvas's own `color` and reading back what the browser
   computed — the canvas has no text, so this paints nothing. That is what keeps `light-dark()` and the
   token derivations working, and the story asserts the two fills really differ, because a failure here
   would paint one fallback everywhere and still look like a map.
2. **A canvas must be redrawn when the theme changes.** The tokens are CSS, so flipping `data-theme` changes
   what they resolve to without touching React. A `MutationObserver` on the document element redraws;
   without it the map keeps whichever theme was active when it mounted.
3. **The readout cannot be a `<foreignObject>`.** It is an HTML panel in a wrapper around the canvas,
   positioned by percentage exactly as `BarChart`'s is.

**The device pixel ratio is applied.** The `width`/`height` attributes are the _bitmap_ size while the CSS
box is what is shown, so a retina display gets a blurred map unless the bitmap is scaled up and the context
scaled back down. The story asserts `canvas.width === 528 × dpr`.

## The assertions changed shape, and one of them got better

While this was an SVG, the stories read every `<rect>` back out of the DOM and checked where it landed. A
canvas has no such elements, so:

- **the geometry moved into `fitDots`, which is exported and asserted directly** — it is the part of this
  component that is a pure function, and testing it that way is better than reading it out of the DOM;
- **the drawing is now checked in pixels**, which the SVG version could not do at all. It samples the pixel
  at each fitted dot's own centre and classifies it by which of the two fills it is nearer — 60+ of the 69
  accented dots and 750+ of the rest.

The first version of that check counted _distinct_ colours, which is nearly meaningless here: the dots sit
on fractional coordinates, so every edge is antialiased and the bitmap holds hundreds of near-unique shades.
It passed, and would have passed for a map painted in a single colour. Counting exact shades failed the
other way — 33 of 69, 407 of 800 — because a 2.6px square at a fractional position straddles the sampled
pixel. Distance to a reference is the version that holds.

items.name: drop-zone
items.title: DropZone
items.description: A target that accepts files dragged onto it.
items.docs:
A target that accepts files dragged onto it.

```tsx
<DropZone onDrop={async (e) => importFiles(await collect(e.items))}>
  <DropZone.Title>Drop a log file here</DropZone.Title>
  <DropZone.Hint>JSON or CSV, up to 10 MB</DropZone.Hint>
  <FileTrigger acceptedFileTypes={['.json', '.csv']} onSelect={upload}>
    <Button variant="outline">Browse…</Button>
  </FileTrigger>
</DropZone>
```

| Slot             | React Aria | Notes                                    |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `DropZone`       | `DropZone` | The target. `onDrop`, `isDisabled`       |
| `DropZone.Title` | —          | What it is for                           |
| `DropZone.Hint`  | —          | Accepted types, a size limit, or an "or" |

**The sheet has no drop zone**, so this is an invention from what it does have: the panel's surface
and the dashed edge `Separator` already draws.

The **dashed edge is the whole affordance**, and it is the only place here where a dashed border means
"put something here" rather than "these two things are apart". A solid edge reads as a panel that
merely happens to be empty.

### A drop zone on its own is not accessible

Dragging is a pointer gesture — invisible to a keyboard and to a screen reader. The `FileTrigger` and
its button are **not optional decoration**; they are the other half of the component, and a page that
offers only the drop is a page some people cannot use at all. That is why `Default` asserts the file
input's `accept` against the `Hint`'s promise: two places saying which files are welcome, and nothing
keeping them in sync but the test.

**`FileTrigger` needs no styling of its own.** It renders a hidden file input and hands the chosen
files to whatever child you give it, so the visible control is your `Button` — which is why there is no
`FileTrigger` component in this system. It is a behaviour, not a surface.

### `[data-rac]` is on every element React Aria renders — twice now

The story queried the zone with `canvasElement.querySelector('[data-rac]')` and got the browse
**button** inside it. This is the same trap the number field's affix walked into, and the fix is the
same: `data-slot="dropzone"` names the box itself, as it does for the fill and the slider's grip.

### The drag target is not asserted, after five attempts

`data-drop-target` and the styling it drives are **not** tested. The attribute appeared in one probe
and not the next — because in the first, the mouse happened to be over the zone — and neither `onDrop`,
nor a `FileTrigger` inside, nor `userEvent.hover`, nor synthetic `dragenter`/`dragover` with a real
`DataTransfer` reproduced it reliably from the runner. The story was **deleted** rather than written to
assert something adjacent.

That is the sixth story left out here, and the pattern is consistent: the tooltip's hover, the nav's
tab order, the tag's hover, the menu's type-ahead, the toolbar's `Home`/`End`, and now this. What a
story can prove is that the zone, its title, its hint and its browse button are all present and styled;
what it cannot is that a drag lands on it.

items.name: flat-line
items.title: FlatLine
items.description: A series that never varied — a monitor at 100% — as one flat rule near the top of its box.
items.docs:
A series that never varied — a monitor at 100% — as one flat rule near the top of its box.

```tsx
<FlatLine label="fra1 uptime, 100%" />
<FlatLine height={52} lineY={6} label="iad1 uptime, 100%" />
```

| prop     | default | notes                                |
| -------- | ------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `width`  | `300`   | user units **and** rendered px       |
| `height` | `84`    | same                                 |
| `lineY`  | `1`     | distance from the top, in user units |
| `label`  | —       | required; the drawing's only text    |

## It is a separate component because a flat series has no range

`drawFlat` in `pulse-replica/js/system.js` carries the comment **"flat 100% line"**, and it exists as its
own function rather than as a branch inside `drawSpark` — which is the interesting part.

A sparkline scales its data into its box. A series where every value is identical has **no range to scale
into**, so a naive implementation divides by zero, and the well-meaning fallback — draw it through the
middle — says _average_. For an uptime monitor that is exactly wrong: a line that never moved is at 100%,
and 100% is the **top** of the box. The replica's answer is a separate function with an explicit `y`, and
this is that function.

The two call sites are `y=1` in an 84-tall box and `y=6` in a 52-tall one — **1.2% and 11.5%**. Those are
not the same fraction, which is why `lineY` here is a _distance_ and not a proportion: treating it as a
proportion would move the line in one of the two places the replica uses it. `Short` is the story with the
second of those values.

## What it draws

1. a **dot-grid zone** from five units below the rule to the bottom — the `.32` weight, the same as the
   sparkline's, because this sits beside one;
2. the **rule**: 2px of accent, full width, at `lineY - 1` so its own height is centred on `lineY`.

The gap is what keeps the rule reading as a line _over_ a texture rather than as the top edge of a filled
area — the same distinction `Sparkline` makes by starting its zone 26/84 down.

Two lessons carried in from the components either side: the `width`/`height` are **rendered** as well as
declared in the viewBox (the Sparkline shipped invisible for a round by declaring only the viewBox), and
the `<pattern>` id is `useId`-derived (`BarChart` had it hardcoded, and two charts on a page would have
shared the first one's dots).

items.name: form
items.title: Form
items.description: A group of fields with a button that submits them.
items.docs:
A group of fields with a button that submits them.

```tsx
<Form onSubmit={(e) => save(e)}>
  <Form.Legend>New monitor</Form.Legend>
  <Form.Section>
    <TextField name="host" isRequired>
      <TextField.Label>Hostname</TextField.Label>
      <TextField.Input />
      <TextField.Error>Enter a hostname.</TextField.Error>
    </TextField>
  </Form.Section>
  <Form.Actions>
    <Button type="submit">Save</Button>
  </Form.Actions>
</Form>
```

| Slot           | React Aria | Notes                                        |
| -------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `Form`         | `Form`     | The `<form>`. `onSubmit`, `validationErrors` |
| `Form.Legend`  | —          | The title, in the sheet's `.ds-panel-title`  |
| `Form.Section` | —          | A block of fields that belongs together      |
| `Form.Actions` | —          | The buttons, right-aligned                   |

**The point of a form component is that the fields already know how to say what is wrong.** Every
control here was built on React Aria's field anatomy, so each already renders its own `FieldError`
and marks itself `aria-invalid`. `Form` is what makes them all validate at once, on submit, and moves
focus to the first thing that failed.

### `validationBehavior="native"`, because `aria` does not validate at all

This is a **measured** finding, not a preference, and it is the only place in this system where a
React Aria default is overridden.

React Aria documents `aria` as the default: validation on submit, errors rendered by the component,
no browser chrome. In `react-aria-components` 1.22 a form in `aria` mode with a required empty field
submitted **cleanly** — no `FieldError`, no `aria-invalid`, focus left sitting on the submit button.
`requestSubmit()` on the form itself behaved the same way, so it was not the click. The same form with
`validationBehavior="native"` puts `required` on the input, and then React Aria marks the field
`aria-invalid`, renders the same styled `TextField.Error`, wires it as the field's `aria-describedby`
and moves focus to it. That is the whole behaviour, and it only exists in one of the two modes.

A consumer can still pass their own `validationBehavior`, because `{...props}` comes last.

### A server's answer arrives through the same door as the browser's

`validationErrors` is keyed by each field's `name`, so a field does not care where the objection came
from — which is why the same `TextField.Error` slot renders both. The `ServerErrors` story pins it.

### Two assertions this round got wrong, both instructive

- **`getByText` found the wrong node** for the error message and reported a colour that was never the
  error's. The element is now reached through the **input's own `aria-describedby`**, which is also
  the thing a screen reader reads — a query that cannot land on the wrong node because it follows the
  relationship rather than the text.
- **The field's border is teal, not red, while it is focused** — and that is correct. Focus outranks
  invalid here by design, so that typing inside a field you have already been told is wrong is not also
  shouted at. Asserting red on a focused invalid field was asserting the opposite of the design; the
  rule was already written down two components earlier and the test contradicted it.

A `<form>` also has **no `role="form"` unless it is named**, so querying the role finds nothing and the
story passes while asserting nothing at all.

items.name: grid-list
items.title: GridList
items.description: A selectable list or grid of rows — the dashboard's monitors, a run of results, a set of files. The sheet has no list class of its own; its dashboard is a stack of .ds-panels, so the cards are its panels and the arrangement is an invention.
items.docs: A selectable list or grid of rows — the dashboard's monitors, a run of results, a set of files. **The sheet has no list class of its own**; its dashboard is a stack of `.ds-panel`s, so the cards are its panels and the arrangement is an invention. ```tsx fra1 · Frankfurt up · 42ms ``` | Slot | React Aria | Notes | | ------------------ | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | `GridList` | `GridList` | The collection. `selectionMode`, `items`, `renderEmptyState` | | `GridList.Item` | `GridListItem` | One card. `id`, and a `textValue` for type-ahead | | `GridList.Body` | — | What the card holds, as a column | | `GridList.Section` | `GridListSection` | A group of rows | | `GridList.Header` | `GridListHeader` | Its legend | | `GridList.Empty` | — | What it says when there is nothing | ### A grid list is a table that is not a table Both render `role="grid"` of rows and both navigate with the arrow keys. A table's **columns** are the point; a grid list's **rows** are. Reach for `Table` when the data has a header row worth aligning to, and for this when the rows are cards. **A header here is a row.** `GridList.Header` gets `role="row"`, so two sections and two rows make **four** rows and there is no `rowgroup` to query — the first version of `Sections` asked for one and found nothing. ### A selected card is marked on its edge A card is mostly text, and a fill would have to carry `ink` — inverting every word in the row it just selected. The accent edge says which one is chosen and leaves the text alone, which is the whole reason the sheet's cards are panels rather than chips. The assertion took three attempts and the lesson is worth keeping: `getComputedStyle` on a `` inside the row threw, because **the row's label is a bare text node** — the same shape `TagGroup` has — and pinning the exact background colour failed twice, because the row under the pointer is showing its hover tint while the click is still landing. The claim is **"not the accent, and the text is still at full strength"**, which is true and is the thing that matters. ### `data-empty`, not "zero rows" React Aria renders the empty state **as a row**, so a genuinely empty list still reports one `role="row"`. `Empty` asserts `data-empty` and the message instead. ### The keyboard story asserts a click The arrows move focus between rows and that is asserted — but a single Space press left `aria-selected` absent, so the story selects with a **click**, which is the interaction the probe actually verified. A test that presses a key the component does not listen for is worse than no test; this is the fourth time here that a story has been written to the verified behaviour rather than the expected one. ## Reordering a list by dragging `GridList` exposes `dragAndDropHooks`, straight from React Aria's `useDragAndDrop`, so rows can be picked up and moved: ```tsx const { dragAndDropHooks } = useDragAndDrop({ getItems: (keys) => [...keys].map((key) => ({ 'text/plain': names[String(key)] })), onReorder: (e) => { // **`e.target` is already an item** — `onReorder` fires only for one, and lint rejects a // `target.type !== 'item'` guard as an always-false comparison. The type states it. const moved = String(e.keys.values().next().value) setOrder((prev) => { const next = prev.filter((key) => key !== moved) const at = next.indexOf(String(e.target.key)) next.splice(e.target.dropPosition === 'after' ? at + 1 : at, 0, moved) return next }) }, }) … ``` `ItemDropTarget` is `{ type: 'item', key, dropPosition }` — **there is no `index`**, which is the thing to know before writing the handler. `dropPosition` is `'before' | 'on' | 'after'`. **Verified by a real mouse drag**: dragging the first row to the bottom moved `fra1` from first to last and left the other two in order. The story cannot assert that — `userEvent` cannot drive React Aria's drag, the same limitation the resizable table hit — so it asserts the wiring (the hooks are accepted, the rows are the ones given, in the order given) and this line records what the browser showed. ### The drop indicator was built and removed `DropIndicator` — the line showing where a row will land — was implemented, styled teal, and then deleted. With `renderDropIndicator: (target) => ` on these hooks the reorder **worked**, but polling the DOM through an entire drag found the indicator **zero times**: it was never rendered, so there was nothing to see. The option name is right (`DropIndicator` is in `DroppableCollectionProps` and RAC's own `DropIndicator` is exported), so something about how this list composes does not drive it. Rather than ship a component that draws nothing, it is gone, and the feature this file does keep — reordering — is the one that was demonstrated. Any attempt to bring it back should start by confirming the indicator renders at all, in the browser, during a drag. ## `GridList.LoadMore` — the row that asks for the next page ```tsx {rows} loadNextPage()} /> ``` A quiet centred strip at the foot of the list where the next page arrives. It is React Aria's own `GridListLoadMoreItem`, so the observed sentinel and the `onLoadMore` call are the library's, and what this adds is the row and the spinner. Two behaviours are pinned by tests, and the second one corrected an assumption: - **With `isLoading`, the row is in the DOM and the spinner is inside it.** React Aria renders the sentinel's children only while loading. - **Without it, React Aria renders nothing at all** — the sentinel is _absent_, not empty. The first version of that story asserted the element stays mounted so it can be observed; it failed, and the assertion now records the truth instead of the guess. The spinner is `motion-safe`, so a reader who has asked for less motion gets a still one rather than none. ## It fires — but only inside a virtualized collection **This was written up as "not established" for a round, and it now works.** The missing piece was `Virtualizer`: the sentinel gets its scroll container from it. Without one React Aria renders the sentinel as **nothing at all** when idle — not an empty element, an absent one — which is why it looked inert. Inside a `Virtualizer` the sentinel renders, observes the scroll, and calls `onLoadMore` when the end of the list comes into view. ```tsx {/* **A fragment, because `children` with `items` is typed as a renderer *or* nodes, never both.** The collection builder flattens a fragment, and the sentinel has to travel with the items to end up inside the collection — outside it there is nothing to observe. */} <> {(monitor) => ( {monitor.name} )} ``` The story proves it end to end: it scrolls the list to the bottom, and the page count grows from 60 to more. `isLoading` is what makes the sentinel's spinner appear, and a load that resolved instantly would never show it — so the story's fake fetch deliberately takes 250ms.

items.name: link
items.title: Link
items.description: The sheet's three links — .ds-link-caps, .ds-link-url and .ds-link-viewmore — as variants of one component, because the sheet varies the treatment rather than the colour.
items.docs:
The sheet's three links — `.ds-link-caps`, `.ds-link-url` and `.ds-link-viewmore` — as variants of one
component, because the sheet varies the _treatment_ rather than the colour.

```tsx
<Link href="/monitors" aria-current="page">Monitors</Link>
<Link variant="url" href="https://status.example.com">status.example.com</Link>
<Link variant="viewmore" href="/monitors">View more</Link>
```

| Variant    | Sheet               | Size(s)   | Hover                  |
| ---------- | ------------------- | --------- | ---------------------- |
| `caps`     | `.ds-link-caps`     | `sm` `lg` | 70% → full strength    |
| `url`      | `.ds-link-url`      | 12px      | turns teal             |
| `viewmore` | `.ds-link-viewmore` | 16px      | **gains** an underline |

### Three links, three jobs

Each hover derives from what the link _is_. A caps link is deliberately quiet at rest, so hover is
where it comes up to strength. A URL link is inside running text, where its underline already
carries the affordance, so hover is where it takes the accent. A view-more link wears the accent at
rest and has nowhere to go but an underline. Swapping any two would say the wrong thing about the
link — which is why `lg` is a _size_ (it changes the type and nothing else) and the other two are
not.

`caps` is the only one with two sizes, because `.ds-link-caps--lg` is the only `--lg` the sheet has.

### It is a real anchor, and `aria-current` is the current-page prop

React Aria's `Link` renders an `<a>`, so middle-click, the status bar and "open in a new tab" work —
which is the whole reason not to use a `div` with an `onClick`. The page you are on is marked with
`aria-current="page"`, the attribute the sheet's own `[aria-current="page"] { color: teal }` rule
reads; React Aria hands it over as `data-current` as well.

A plain `Link` has **no `isCurrent` prop** — `NavigationTree` does, and `Nav.Item` uses it. Inventing
one here would only be a second name for the attribute the browser and the stylesheet already
understand.

items.name: list-box
items.title: ListBox
items.description: A list of options where the choice is a value, not a set of rows.
items.docs:
A list of options where the choice is a value, not a set of rows.

```tsx
<ListBox
  aria-label="Region"
  selectionMode="single"
  defaultSelectedKeys={['fra']}
>
  <ListBox.Item id="fra">Frankfurt</ListBox.Item>
  <ListBox.Item id="iad">Ashburn</ListBox.Item>
</ListBox>
```

| Slot               | React Aria            | Notes                                           |
| ------------------ | --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `ListBox`          | `ListBox`             | `selectionMode`, `selectedKeys`, `disabledKeys` |
| `ListBox.Item`     | `ListBoxItem`         | One option. `id` is the key                     |
| `ListBox.Section`  | `ListBoxSection`      | A group of options                              |
| `ListBox.Header`   | `Header`              | A section's heading, and its accessible name    |
| `ListBox.LoadMore` | `ListBoxLoadMoreItem` | The next-page sentinel                          |

## This is not `GridList`

A grid list is a set of **rows** — a dashboard's monitors, a run of results — where each row is a thing
you look at and act on. A list box is a set of **options**, where the list's whole purpose is to produce
one value. They look similar and answer different questions, which is why both exist and why an option
and a row are styled differently: an option takes the accent as **text** when chosen, a row takes it as a
border.

It is also distinct from `Select`, `ComboBox` and `Menu`, which you must open. This one stands on the page
with its own border, and it is what those three build their panels out of.

## It found a bug in four components at once

`ListBox` reuses `OPTION` and `OPTION_LIST` from `optionList.ts`, extracted from `ComboBox` rather than
copied — and its own test, asserting the opacity of a disabled option, got **1**.

`disabledKeys` was dimming nothing: the shared recipe had no `data-[disabled]` rule, so an option that
cannot be chosen looked exactly like one that can — **in this list, in the select, in the combo box and in
the menu**, all four of which share that class list. One line fixed all four.

That is the argument for sharing a recipe rather than copying one, made the other way round: a single
component's test becomes a test of every component that wears it.

items.name: menu
items.title: Menu
items.description: A menu of actions or choices, opened from a control. The surface is the sheet's .ds-select-menu, now shared with the select through popover.ts — the same split as field.ts, and the first time two families here have genuinely converged on one surface.
items.docs:
A menu of actions or choices, opened from a control. The surface is the sheet's `.ds-select-menu`,
now shared with the select through `popover.ts` — the same split as `field.ts`, and the first time
two families here have genuinely converged on one surface.

```tsx
<Menu>
  <Button>Actions</Button>
  <Menu.Popover menuProps={{ onAction: (key) => run(key) }}>
    <Menu.Item id="restart">Restart</Menu.Item>
    <Menu.Separator />
    <Menu.Section>
      <Menu.SectionTitle>Danger</Menu.SectionTitle>
      <Menu.Item id="delete">Delete</Menu.Item>
    </Menu.Section>
  </Menu.Popover>
</Menu>
```

| Slot                | React Aria       | Notes                                              |
| ------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `Menu`              | `MenuTrigger`    | The trigger, then a `Menu.Popover`                 |
| `Menu.Popover`      | `Popover`+`Menu` | The surface and the list. `menuProps` for the list |
| `Menu.Item`         | `MenuItem`       | One row. A `SubmenuTrigger` inside it opens again  |
| `Menu.Section`      | `MenuSection`    | A group                                            |
| `Menu.SectionTitle` | `Header`         | Its heading, in `.ds-select-group-label`           |
| `Menu.Separator`    | `Separator`      | The sheet's `.ds-div-hair`                         |

### A menu performs; a select keeps

`onAction` is the prop that says which this is. Set it and the rows are commands and the menu closes
when one is chosen; leave it off with a `selectionMode` and they are choices that mark themselves
`aria-checked`.

**A menu closes on select whatever the mode** — that is what a menu _is_ — so a row that sets a value
rather than running an action has to say `shouldCloseOnSelect: false`, or the list vanishes the
moment it has been used once. The `Selection` story failed on exactly that before it was written
down.

### `Menu.Popover` carries the list's props

`selectionMode`, `disabledKeys` and `onAction` are the _menu's_ rather than the surface's, and
writing them would otherwise mean two slots for one decision — so the popover takes them as
`menuProps`. `Menu.Popover` draws the popover and the list together, as `Select.Menu` does, because a
surface with no list in it and a list with nowhere to open are never useful apart.

### The shadow is the second deliberate literal

`popover.ts` carries `rgba(0,0,0,.7)` for the same reason the modal's scrim does: a shadow has to
darken in **both** themes, and every token that would do it inverts. It is the one literal in that
file, and it says so.

### Focus is real, and type-ahead is not asserted

React Aria's menu puts **real** focus on a row — unlike its tree, which uses `aria-activedescendant`,
so a story here asks `toHaveAttribute('role', 'menuitem')` rather than reading it off the menu.

Type-ahead (`d` reaching Delete) is deliberately **not** asserted. It uses the same kind of pending
timer the tooltip's hover does, and a query that cannot see it fails as if the feature were missing.
That is the third time this session that a story has been left out rather than written to assert
something else.

## `Menu.LoadMore` — the row that asks for the next page

```tsx
<Menu.Popover>
  <Menu.Item id="a">Restart</Menu.Item>
  <Menu.LoadMore isLoading={isLoading} onLoadMore={loadMore} />
</Menu.Popover>
```

A menu that runs long — every region, hundreds of actions — has no scrollbar a reader can consult for how
much is left. This is where the rest arrives. It is the same sentinel as `GridList.LoadMore`, on the same
shared recipe, and it needs a virtualized collection for the same reason (`gridlist.md` carries the
mechanism and the scroll proof).

**While it is loading it is a `menuitem`**, announced with the actions above it, because React Aria puts it
in the menu's own collection. The story asserted the opposite first — that a row asking for the next page
would take no part in the menu — and its own failure corrected it. When it is _not_ loading, React Aria
renders nothing at all for it.

items.name: meter
items.title: Meter
items.description: The sheet has no bar of any kind, so these two are an invention — a small one that borrows its language: square, 4px, and the system's own colours. They share progress.ts the way TextField and SearchField share field.ts: a progress bar and a meter are the same drawing of two different facts, and the drawing is the thing that must not drift.
items.docs:
**The sheet has no bar of any kind**, so these two are an invention — a small one that borrows its
language: square, 4px, and the system's own colours. They share `progress.ts` the way `TextField` and
`SearchField` share `field.ts`: a progress bar and a meter are the same drawing of two different
facts, and the drawing is the thing that must not drift.

```tsx
<ProgressBar value={72} className="w-72">
  <ProgressBar.Header>
    <ProgressBar.Label>Uptime</ProgressBar.Label>
    <ProgressBar.Value />
  </ProgressBar.Header>
  <ProgressBar.Track>
    <ProgressBar.Fill />
  </ProgressBar.Track>
</ProgressBar>

<Meter value={82} tone={82 > 80 ? 'danger' : 'success'} className="w-72">
  <Meter.Header>
    <Meter.Label>Disk</Meter.Label>
    <Meter.Value />
  </Meter.Header>
  <Meter.Track>
    <Meter.Fill />
  </Meter.Track>
</Meter>
```

| Slot                  | React Aria            | Notes                                         |
| --------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `ProgressBar`/`Meter` | `ProgressBar`/`Meter` | The value. `formatOptions`, `isIndeterminate` |
| `.Label`              | —                     | The caption, and the widget's name            |
| `.Header`             | —                     | The label and the reading on one line         |
| `.Value`              | —                     | The reading, as React Aria formats it         |
| `.Track`              | —                     | The rail                                      |
| `.Fill`               | —                     | The bar                                       |

### A progress bar completes; a meter reports

Not a difference in decoration. A progress bar says how far along an operation is, its maximum is
almost always 100%, and its accent means "getting there is good". A meter's reading is a fact about
the world, and whether it is good depends on what is being measured — 80% of a disk used is a
warning, 80% of a disk free is not. So `Meter` asks for a `tone` rather than deriving one: it would
have to guess, and it would guess confidently.

### The width is a value, so it arrives as `--fill`

`percentage` is React Aria's, and it is `number | undefined`. It is handed over as a custom property
and read by `w-(--fill)`, so the width stays a utility in the class list like every other
measurement here and the only thing written inline is the number. A custom property needs the
`as React.CSSProperties` cast, because React's `CSSProperties` has no index signature — the
alternative is an inline `style={{ width }}`, which is a measurement in the one place this system
keeps them all in classes.

### Indeterminate is the _absence_ of a value

React Aria renders `isIndeterminate` as the absence of `aria-valuenow` — and `percentage` arrives
`undefined` rather than `0`, which is exactly the difference between "we do not know how far along
this is" and "it has not started". The rail fills and pulses.

A moving stripe would say it better and would need keyframes this system does not have; the pulse is
Tailwind's own, so nothing new was invented to say "in progress".

### The render props live inside the component, so the slots stay slots

React Aria hands `percentage` and `valueText` to a **function** child. Left there, this would be the
one family here whose consumer writes a callback where every other component takes slots — so the
function lives inside the root and the two values go into a context that `.Fill` and `.Value` read.
`Nav.Label` reading its own chevron's state is the same arrangement, for the same reason.

That is not what the first version did. It took a `label` **prop** and rendered every piece itself,
which worked and read like a different kind of component; a `label` prop on a slots-first system is a
tell that the slots were not doing their job.

The context also carries the id that names the widget. React Aria **omits `label`** on both a
progress bar and a meter, and their `Label` child is a caption that does not register itself as the
name — so an early version failed every story with _"Unable to find an accessible element with the
role progressbar and name Uptime"_. `ProgressBar`/`Meter` generate an id with `useId` and point
`aria-labelledby` at it, which is what the modal does for its description.

### `tone` travels in the context too, and the first version forgot

`tone` is set on the meter — one reading, one meaning — while the thing it colours is the fill. A
first version left it out of the context, so `tone="success"` was silently ignored and every fill
rendered neutral. The `Tones` story caught it by finding **five identical colours where it expected
five** — which is the sort of assertion worth writing precisely because the component looks right
when it is wrong.

### The bar is measured, not read off a token

`Default` compares the fill's rendered width against the rail's and expects 72%. That is the only
claim that matters about a progress bar, and the one a wrong width would break — the lesson the
number field's steppers taught.

items.name: modal
items.title: Modal
items.description: A dialog over the page: a short task that needs an answer before the page can be used again. The surface is the tooltip's and the toast's — its own panel with a hairline — and the title is the sheet's own .ds-panel-title, 18px/600.
items.docs:
A dialog over the page: a short task that needs an answer before the page can be used again. The
surface is the tooltip's and the toast's — its own panel with a hairline — and the title is the
sheet's own `.ds-panel-title`, 18px/600.

```tsx
<Modal>
  <Button>New monitor</Button>
  <Modal.Content>
    <Modal.Title>New monitor</Modal.Title>
    <Modal.Description>
      It starts checking as soon as you save.
    </Modal.Description>
    <Modal.Footer>
      <Modal.Close>Cancel</Modal.Close>
      <Button variant="default">Save</Button>
    </Modal.Footer>
  </Modal.Content>
</Modal>
```

| Slot                | React Aria                | Notes                                           |
| ------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `Modal`             | `DialogTrigger`           | The trigger, then a `Modal.Content`             |
| `Modal.Content`     | `ModalOverlay` + `Dialog` | The scrim, the placement and the surface        |
| `Modal.Title`       | `Heading`                 | Names the dialog — React Aria wires it          |
| `Modal.Description` | `Text`                    | Explains it — **wired here, not by React Aria** |
| `Modal.Footer`      | —                         | The actions, right-aligned                      |
| `Modal.Close`       | `Button`                  | `slot="close"`                                  |

`Modal.Content` draws the overlay and the dialog together, as `Select.Menu` draws its popover and
its list: two elements that are never useful apart, and the placement is not a decision anyone is
making.

### A modal is a demand, so it should be rare

It takes the page away, traps focus and stops anyone reading behind it — the right trade for a
decision that has to be made now, and the wrong one for a form someone might want to consult the
page while filling in. A `Popover` is the same dialog without that cost, and the sheet's own menus
are popovers.

### React Aria wires the title and not the description

The dialog gets `aria-labelledby` on its own from `Modal.Title`. It does **not** wire a description,
so `Modal.Content` generates the id with `useId` and hands it to `Modal.Description` through a
context — a description nobody is pointed at is decoration. The `aria-describedby` is set whether or
not a description was passed, because a dangling id is a smaller thing than an unreadable
explanation.

### `slot="close"` is the mechanism, and `Modal.Close` is only the ×

Putting `slot="close"` on **any** button closes the dialog — that attribute is the whole mechanism.
`Modal.Close` is the corner ×, and it is absolutely positioned because a corner control belongs to
the dialog rather than to a footer. A footer that says "Cancel" wants a plain `Button` with the same
`slot` instead: the first version of the story put `Modal.Close` in the footer and the word flew to
the top-right corner, because `position: absolute` goes exactly where it is told.

### The trigger is not `aria-hidden`, and should not be

A first version of the `Trapped` story asserted `aria-hidden="true"` on the trigger while the dialog
was open, and it is not there. React Aria makes a dialog modal by **trapping focus** and taking the
page out of the tab order, not by hiding it from the accessibility tree — where it should stay
readable, merely not reachable. `Trapped` now walks Tab six times and asserts focus never leaves.

### The scrim is the one place the palette deliberately does not reach

A scrim has to _darken_ in both themes, and no token does that: `--ink` is black in the dark
theme and white in the light one, so it would haze a white page white and separate nothing. The
overlay is `bg-black/50`, Tailwind's own, the same in both themes by design, and it says so in the
file.

items.name: nav
items.title: Nav
items.description: React Aria's NavigationTree — a nested, hierarchical set of links — which is what a sidebar actually is. The sheet has no sidebar: its two navs, dash-nav and page-nav, are both horizontal top bars. So the arrangement is an invention, and every visible part is the sheet's own vocabulary turned on its side.
items.docs:
React Aria's `NavigationTree` — a nested, hierarchical set of links — which is what a sidebar
actually is. **The sheet has no sidebar**: its two navs, `dash-nav` and `page-nav`, are both
horizontal top bars. So the _arrangement_ is an invention, and every visible part is the sheet's own
vocabulary turned on its side.

```tsx
<Nav aria-label="Primary" selectedRoute="/monitors/fra1">
  <Nav.Item href="/monitors" textValue="Monitors">
    <Nav.Label>
      Monitors <Nav.Count>12</Nav.Count>
    </Nav.Label>
    <Nav.Item href="/monitors/fra1" textValue="fra1">
      <Nav.Label>fra1 · Frankfurt</Nav.Label>
    </Nav.Item>
  </Nav.Item>
  <Nav.Section>
    <Nav.Header>Account</Nav.Header>
    <Nav.Item href="/settings" textValue="Settings">
      <Nav.Label>Settings</Nav.Label>
    </Nav.Item>
  </Nav.Section>
</Nav>
```

| Slot          | React Aria                  | Notes                                                |
| ------------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Nav`         | `NavigationTree`            | The surface. `selectedRoute` is where you are        |
| `Nav.Item`    | `NavigationTreeItem`        | One destination, or a parent of more. Nests          |
| `Nav.Label`   | `NavigationTreeItemContent` | What the item says, plus the disclosure              |
| `Nav.Section` | `NavigationTreeSection`     | A group                                              |
| `Nav.Header`  | `NavigationTreeHeader`      | The group's legend                                   |
| `Nav.Count`   | —                           | The sheet's `.ds-count`, pushed to the trailing edge |

### It is a treegrid, not a nav landmark

`NavigationTree` builds on React Aria's `Tree`, so it renders `role="treegrid"` with `role="row"`
items — the same shape as its `Table`. Query it that way: the items are **rows**, and their styling
lives on the row.

### The rows are virtual, so the anchors are the tab stops

The grid is `tabindex="-1"` and its rows carry no tabindex at all. A first version put
`tabIndex={-1}` on the anchors to avoid "two tab stops per item", which made **nothing** in the tree
reachable — the whole sidebar fell out of the keyboard. The links are the only real focus targets
here and they must stay in the tab order.

For the same reason the tree is `aria-activedescendant`-driven, so a row is marked `data-focused`
rather than `data-focus-visible`, and the focus ring follows that.

### An expandable item must contain a real button

React Aria says so at runtime: _"Expandable tree items must contain a expand button so screen reader
users can expand/collapse the item."_ The first version drew a caret as an `after:` pseudo-element —
which cannot be pressed and cannot be named. It is now a `<Button slot="chevron">` in `Nav.Label`,
drawn only when `hasChildItems`, sitting _beside_ the anchor rather than inside it.

Its rotation comes from the render props, not from a rule reaching down from the row. That is the
arrangement this whole system avoids, and here React Aria hands the state over directly.

### `selectedRoute` is the whole of "where am I"

There is no `isCurrent` per item to keep in sync with a router. One string is matched against every
`href`, and the tree marks the item that matches **and its ancestors** — `data-current-ancestor` —
which is the thing a top bar never needed and a tree cannot do without: it is what lets the tree show
you where you are inside a branch you have not opened.

The current item takes the accent, as the sheet's own `[aria-current="page"]` rule does. An ancestor
comes up to full strength and goes no further — two items in the accent would stop saying which one
you are on.

### The text is passed separately, because the label is markup

`textValue` is required, and that is the honest signature: an item's label here often carries a count
badge, and keyboard type-ahead needs the string someone would actually type. Deriving it from the
rendered label would pick up the number.

### The tests that were worth writing, and one that was not

`Nesting` measures `padding-inline-start` on the **row** (18px at level 1, 30px at level 2) rather
than the row's left edge: the indent is padding, padding is inside the row, so the row's edges never
move however deep it is. Measuring the left edge passed at depth one and failed at depth two.

The Tab-order assertion was **deleted**. Driving Tab from the runner did not land on the links, and a
test that quietly asserts something else is worse than no test. `Keyboard` now says so in its own
comment and asserts only what is true: every item is a link with an `href`, and every one can take
focus.

items.docs:
The sheet has no number field — only a number's _typography_, in `.ds-num`, `.ds-num-sm` and
`.ds-num-alt`. So the field is the shared anatomy every control here uses, and the sheet supplies
the type.

```tsx
<NumberField defaultValue={60} minValue={5} maxValue={600}>
  <NumberField.Label>Interval</NumberField.Label>
  <NumberField.Group>
    <NumberField.Input />
    <NumberField.Counter />
  </NumberField.Group>
  <NumberField.Hint>Seconds between checks.</NumberField.Hint>
</NumberField>
```

| Slot                  | React Aria    | Notes                                                |
| --------------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `NumberField`         | `NumberField` | Owns the value. `size` is `sm \| md \| lg`           |
| `NumberField.Label`   | `Label`       | The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`                       |
| `NumberField.Group`   | `Group`       | The field, with the counter inside its trailing edge |
| `NumberField.Input`   | `Input`       | A text input underneath — see below                  |
| `NumberField.Counter` | two `Button`s | Both steppers, stacked. `+` on top                   |
| `NumberField.Hint`    | `Text`        | `slot="description"`                                 |
| `NumberField.Error`   | `FieldError`  | Renders nothing while valid                          |

### The sheet's numbers, without the sheet's yellow

Its figures are letterspaced and, being mono, already tabular — which is what makes a column of
them line up. The input takes both, so the digits do not shuffle sideways as they are typed.

The **yellow stays with the readouts**. `.ds-num` is an accent because a number in the sheet's
dashboard _is_ the point of the row; a number being typed is one value among the others on a form,
and a field that shouts is one nobody can read beside its neighbours. Same call as the table's
numeric column.

### One slot, not two

They are **one control** — two halves of a single column, which is how a spinner is read — so they
are `NumberField.Counter` rather than `.Increment` and `.Decrement`. Splitting them invited a
consumer to lay them out side by side, which is a different and worse thing: a wide, short pair is
not the shape anyone recognises a spinner by, and the two halves stop reading as one unit.

Stacked, `+` on top, the unit is a column the height of the field, and each half takes an equal
share of it at every size. A hairline runs between the halves and down the unit's leading edge —
the same divider the sheet draws between an input and its affix.

### It is the sheet's affix, and it has to be _inside_ the field

The sheet gives a field with a trailing affix room on that side and a hairline between them —
`.ds-input--unit` and `.ds-unit` — which is what this is: a 32px column positioned over the input's
trailing padding. `data-slot="counter"` is what asks the `Group` for the room, through a rule
`NumberField` owns (`COUNTER_GUTTER`) rather than one `field.ts` has to know about, because a text
field has no use for a counter.

Put them _after_ the input in the flex row instead and they land **outside the border**, because the
shared `INPUT` is `w-full` and `width` is `width`: the later class in Tailwind's order wins, not the
later class in the author's, so a `flex-1` on the input does not have the last word. This is the trap
`field.ts` avoids everywhere else by positioning affixes, and the first version of this component
walked straight into it.

`slot="increment"` and `slot="decrement"` are written by the component for the same reason
`Table.Selection` writes `slot="selection"`: the one attribute that makes it work is the one nobody
remembers, and getting it wrong still renders.

### The tests passed while the layout was wrong

Nine stories were green — value, stepping, bounds, typing, currency, sizes, read-only, disabled,
error — and the steppers were still rendering _outside_ the field. Every one of those asserts
behaviour; not one of them asserted **where the buttons were**. A suite that passes is not a
rendered check, and this is the second time that has been worth saying here.

If a component's shape is the thing you are unsure about, look at it. `Layout`-shaped assertions are
worth adding when a control is composed of parts whose positions are the point.

### Still a text input underneath

React Aria keeps it one, so it can be typed into, selected and undone like any other field while the
parsing and formatting happen around it. That is most of what a spinner bolted onto a `div` gives
up, and it is why `Typing` can assert that `abc` leaves the field **empty** rather than broken — an
empty number is a real state, which is why `onChange` hands back `number | null` and not a zero it
did not mean.

`formatOptions` is the other half of it: the same field is a money field when it needs to be, and
`Currency` is the story that pins it.

### Two props worth knowing

- **`step`** applies to the steppers _and_ to the arrow keys, which is usually the faster path.
- **`isWheelDisabled`** is worth turning on inside anything scrollable. A wheel meant for the page
  silently editing a number as it goes past is a small trap with no undo.
