items.title: OverlayArrow
items.description: The marker that points from a floating panel back at the thing that opened it.
items.docs:
The marker that points from a floating panel back at the thing that opened it. ```tsx

Anchored to the button.

 ``` | Slot | React Aria | Notes | | --------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------- | | `Popover.Arrow` | `OverlayArrow` | Opt-in; inside the popover | | `Tooltip.Arrow` | `OverlayArrow` | Opt-in; inside the tooltip content | ## Nothing uses one by default, and that is a decision A pointer is a shape the design language does not otherwise contain. The sheet's panels are flat rectangles joined to their trigger by proximity and position, and every menu, select and tooltip here opens anchored without one — so it is neither in `popover.ts` nor built into `Popover`. It was left out for three rounds on **inference**, which is a weak reason. Building it as an **opt-in slot** settles the question with code instead: if nothing uses it, the judgement is confirmed; if something needs it, it is already there. That is the difference between a decision and a guess. ## A rotated square, not a triangle ```tsx // The shape's own class list, and the reason it is a separate element: 'block size-2 rotate-45 border-border-strong bg-card' '[[data-placement=bottom]_&]:border-t [[data-placement=bottom]_&]:border-l' ``` Two hairlines and the panel's own fill continue the panel's edge out to a point — the same squared geometry as every other surface here. An SVG arrow would be the one curved thing in the system. Which two edges are kept depends on where React Aria put the overlay, reported as `data-placement` on the **parent** — hence arbitrary ancestor variants rather than plain `data-[…]` ones. ## Two things that cost a round **React Aria owns the outer element's `transform`.** It positions the arrow with an inline `transform`, and an inline style outranks every class — so a `rotate-45` written on that element type-checks, reads correctly in the source, and does nothing. The first version did exactly that and drew an unrotated square. The rotation lives on a `` inside it. This is the third time in this repo an inline style has silently beaten a class. **Tailwind v4 writes the `rotate` property, not `transform`.** The assertion that caught the first bug then reported `transform: 'none'` for an element that _was_ visibly rotated, because `rotate-45` sets `rotate: 45deg`. The code was right and the assertion was wrong. Check `rotate`. ## Focus is the reliable way into a tooltip `Tooltip.Arrow`'s story focuses the trigger with `tab()` rather than hovering it. A tooltip must open for a keyboard user with no pointer, so focus is the first-class route — and it is also the one that does not depend on a hover delay.

items.name: popover
items.title: Popover
items.description: A panel anchored to the thing that opened it, that does not take the page away.
items.docs:
A panel anchored to the thing that opened it, that does not take the page away.

```tsx
<Popover>
  <Button>Filters</Button>
  <Popover.Content placement="bottom start">
    <Popover.Title>Filters</Popover.Title>
    <Popover.Description>Applies to this view only.</Popover.Description>
  </Popover.Content>
</Popover>
```

| Slot                  | React Aria           | Notes                                           |
| --------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `Popover`             | `DialogTrigger`      | The trigger, then a `Popover.Content`           |
| `Popover.Content`     | `Popover` + `Dialog` | The surface, and the dialog that names it       |
| `Popover.Title`       | `Heading`            | The modal's own title type, imported not copied |
| `Popover.Description` | `Text`               | `aria-describedby` wired here, as on Modal      |

**A popover is a modal that is not modal**, and that is the whole decision. It is dismissed by Escape
and by a click outside, but it traps nothing and hides nothing: the page behind stays readable and
usable. Reach for `Modal` when the page is irrelevant to the decision and for this when it is the
context.

The surface is `popover.ts`'s, but **not `POPOVER` itself** — that one is `w-(--trigger-width)`, which
is right for a select matched to its field and wrong for a panel with its own idea of how wide it
should be. It is what `Menu`, `Select` and `ComboBox` are built on; this is the same surface with no
list at all.

**Placement is a request, not an instruction.** `placement="bottom start"` opens downwards when there
is room and flips when there is not, so the story asserts that React Aria reports where the panel
landed rather than the value the prop asked for.

### The browser probe reports "open on load", and is wrong

Worth writing down because it has now happened twice and cost a component once.

A throwaway Playwright script that navigates straight to an `iframe.html?viewMode=story` URL and then
looks for `role="dialog"` **finds one already open**, for both the sheet and the popover — because
Storybook has restored that story's canvas from a previous visit in the same browser context. The
test runner does not: `Default` clicks the trigger and its **first** assertion, made before any click,
is that no dialog is present — and it passes.

**So the runner is the authority on whether something opens by itself, and the probe is not.** The
`Sheet` was removed on this evidence in an earlier round; its size defect was independently confirmed
and stands, but the "opens before you open it" half of that verdict may well have been this artifact.
Trust the suite for state, the screenshot for appearance.

items.name: progress-bar
items.title: ProgressBar
items.description: The sheet has no bar of any kind, so these two are an invention — a small one that borrows its language: square, 4px, and the system's own colours. They share progress.ts the way TextField and SearchField share field.ts: a progress bar and a meter are the same drawing of two different facts, and the drawing is the thing that must not drift.
items.docs:
**The sheet has no bar of any kind**, so these two are an invention — a small one that borrows its
language: square, 4px, and the system's own colours. They share `progress.ts` the way `TextField` and
`SearchField` share `field.ts`: a progress bar and a meter are the same drawing of two different
facts, and the drawing is the thing that must not drift.

```tsx
<ProgressBar value={72} className="w-72">
  <ProgressBar.Header>
    <ProgressBar.Label>Uptime</ProgressBar.Label>
    <ProgressBar.Value />
  </ProgressBar.Header>
  <ProgressBar.Track>
    <ProgressBar.Fill />
  </ProgressBar.Track>
</ProgressBar>

<Meter value={82} tone={82 > 80 ? 'danger' : 'success'} className="w-72">
  <Meter.Header>
    <Meter.Label>Disk</Meter.Label>
    <Meter.Value />
  </Meter.Header>
  <Meter.Track>
    <Meter.Fill />
  </Meter.Track>
</Meter>
```

| Slot                  | React Aria            | Notes                                         |
| --------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `ProgressBar`/`Meter` | `ProgressBar`/`Meter` | The value. `formatOptions`, `isIndeterminate` |
| `.Label`              | —                     | The caption, and the widget's name            |
| `.Header`             | —                     | The label and the reading on one line         |
| `.Value`              | —                     | The reading, as React Aria formats it         |
| `.Track`              | —                     | The rail                                      |
| `.Fill`               | —                     | The bar                                       |

### A progress bar completes; a meter reports

Not a difference in decoration. A progress bar says how far along an operation is, its maximum is
almost always 100%, and its accent means "getting there is good". A meter's reading is a fact about
the world, and whether it is good depends on what is being measured — 80% of a disk used is a
warning, 80% of a disk free is not. So `Meter` asks for a `tone` rather than deriving one: it would
have to guess, and it would guess confidently.

### The width is a value, so it arrives as `--fill`

`percentage` is React Aria's, and it is `number | undefined`. It is handed over as a custom property
and read by `w-(--fill)`, so the width stays a utility in the class list like every other
measurement here and the only thing written inline is the number. A custom property needs the
`as React.CSSProperties` cast, because React's `CSSProperties` has no index signature — the
alternative is an inline `style={{ width }}`, which is a measurement in the one place this system
keeps them all in classes.

### Indeterminate is the _absence_ of a value

React Aria renders `isIndeterminate` as the absence of `aria-valuenow` — and `percentage` arrives
`undefined` rather than `0`, which is exactly the difference between "we do not know how far along
this is" and "it has not started". The rail fills and pulses.

A moving stripe would say it better and would need keyframes this system does not have; the pulse is
Tailwind's own, so nothing new was invented to say "in progress".

### The render props live inside the component, so the slots stay slots

React Aria hands `percentage` and `valueText` to a **function** child. Left there, this would be the
one family here whose consumer writes a callback where every other component takes slots — so the
function lives inside the root and the two values go into a context that `.Fill` and `.Value` read.
`Nav.Label` reading its own chevron's state is the same arrangement, for the same reason.

That is not what the first version did. It took a `label` **prop** and rendered every piece itself,
which worked and read like a different kind of component; a `label` prop on a slots-first system is a
tell that the slots were not doing their job.

The context also carries the id that names the widget. React Aria **omits `label`** on both a
progress bar and a meter, and their `Label` child is a caption that does not register itself as the
name — so an early version failed every story with _"Unable to find an accessible element with the
role progressbar and name Uptime"_. `ProgressBar`/`Meter` generate an id with `useId` and point
`aria-labelledby` at it, which is what the modal does for its description.

### `tone` travels in the context too, and the first version forgot

`tone` is set on the meter — one reading, one meaning — while the thing it colours is the fill. A
first version left it out of the context, so `tone="success"` was silently ignored and every fill
rendered neutral. The `Tones` story caught it by finding **five identical colours where it expected
five** — which is the sort of assertion worth writing precisely because the component looks right
when it is wrong.

### The bar is measured, not read off a token

`Default` compares the fill's rendered width against the rail's and expects 72%. That is the only
claim that matters about a progress bar, and the one a wrong width would break — the lesson the
number field's steppers taught.

items.name: radio
items.title: Radio
items.description: Two controls, one anatomy. Each is a control, and each carries the group it belongs to as a slot — so the compound form covers the whole control, not just its decorations
items.docs:
They look like the obvious API — `RadioButton` is even named like a member — and they are **React Aria's
internal renderers**. `Radio` ends with:

```tsx
<InternalRadioContext.Provider
  value={{ ...aria, inputRef, defaultClassName: 'react-aria-Radio' }}
>
  <RadioButton {...props} ref={ref} />
</InternalRadioContext.Provider>
```

So `RadioButton` **is** the implementation of `Radio`, and `Radio` passes its own `children` down to it. A
`RadioButton` written inside a `Radio` is therefore rendered _as well as_ the one `Radio` builds itself, and
the member ends up with two hidden inputs. The measurement: `getAllByRole('radio')` returned **6 for a group of three**.
That was taken while a `Radio` segment variant existed; the variant is gone, but the double input is not —
it belongs to `RadioButton`, and a plain group reproduces it just as well. The same holds for `CheckboxButton` and `Checkbox`.

**`RadioButton` is therefore not something to consume.** A wrapper around it was written first, could not be
used as intended, and was deleted — `RadioButtonProps` does not even accept a `value`, which is the first clue.
It was briefly reached for again as a `variant="segment"` on `Radio`; that variant has been removed, and the
reason it had to wrap `Radio` rather than `RadioButton` is the paragraph above.

## Two assertions that could not fail, and a real bug

**`getByRole('radio')` returns the visually hidden `input`, not the painted control.** It carries the
semantics and is a transparent pixel box; the painted thing is the `label` around it. Two versions of the
assertion measured the input and reported transparent against a control that was correctly checked on screen.
The version that holds queries the **state** — `label[data-selected]` — rather than indexing into a list whose
order the DOM never promised.

**One version compared a value with itself** (`chosen === chosen`), which cannot fail and therefore asserted
nothing while looking like a check on the fill. It was written by the same hand that has been criticising
exactly this all session.

The bug hiding under all of it: `Radio.Group` carried **both** `flex-col` (from its base) and `flex-row` (added
for horizontal), so which direction won depended on the order Tailwind generated the two utilities in — not
on the class list. The direction is now chosen in one place.

## The parts — including `Radio.Indicator`, which this file never mentioned

Every slot the compound exports, and what each one is for:

| slot              | element | notes                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Radio.Indicator` | `span`  | **the round control** — `aria-hidden`, with a `centre` slot for the dot |
| `Radio.Text`      | `span`  | the label                                                               |
| `Radio.Label`     | `label` | the field label, for the group                                          |
| `Radio.Hint`      | `span`  | the quiet line under the group                                          |
| `Radio.Error`     | `span`  | the error line, when the group is invalid                               |

```tsx
<Radio.Group defaultValue="1h">
  <Radio value="1h">
    <Radio.Indicator />
    <Radio.Text>1h</Radio.Text>
  </Radio>
  <Radio value="24h">
    <Radio.Indicator />
    <Radio.Text>24h</Radio.Text>
  </Radio>
</Radio.Group>
```

**`Radio.Indicator` is not optional in practice, and that is the thing this document got wrong.** React Aria's
`Radio` renders exactly the children it is given and nothing else — there is no default dot. A `Radio` written
without an `Indicator` is therefore a **label with no visible control**: it is focusable, announced, and
invisible. Every example in this file used a `segment` variant — since removed — and that variant was the one
case where omitting the indicator is correct, because a segment's fill _is_ its indicator. So the base anatomy
never appeared, the dot was never documented, and the omission that was right in the one case was wrong in
every other.

That is not a styling detail to infer from a screenshot. It is the difference between a form a reader can fill
in and one they cannot see.

items.name: range-calendar
items.title: RangeCalendar
items.description: Two months at once, with a span of days between them.
items.docs:
Two months at once, with a span of days between them.

```tsx
<RangeCalendar aria-label="Range" />
<RangeCalendar aria-label="Range" defaultValue={{ start, end }} />
```

| Slot                    | React Aria      | Notes                             |
| ----------------------- | --------------- | --------------------------------- |
| `RangeCalendar`         | `RangeCalendar` | The range. `months` defaults to 2 |
| `RangeCalendar.Heading` | —               | The months' names, `aria-hidden`  |
| `RangeCalendar.Cell`    | `CalendarCell`  | One day, with the ends marked     |

**`DateRangePicker` is this inside a popover.** Same chrome, same `DATE_CELL`, same segments — a day
looks the same wherever it is drawn, which is what `date.tsx` exists for.

**A range is two endpoints and everything between them**, which is more state than a single date: the
first click sets the start and it waits, the second sets the end, a third starts over. `CalendarCell`
puts `data-selection-start` and `data-selection-end` on the ends only, so the ends and the days between
them can be styled apart — the span is what makes a range readable at a glance rather than two loose
dates.

**Two months by default.** A range that crosses a month boundary is the normal case, not the exception,
and one month makes the user page back and forth to see what they just selected.

### A range calendar has its own state context

`RangeCalendarStateContext`, not `CalendarStateContext`. Both are provided, and the wrong one does not
throw — it simply carries no `visibleRange`, so the heading rendered **empty**: a blank caption above a
perfectly correct grid. `DatePicker` uses the first and `DateRangePicker` the second, and the difference
is invisible until the heading is missing.

items.name: search-field
items.title: SearchField
items.description: The sheet's .ds-affix--search. The same field anatomy as TextField, but on React Aria's SearchField, so the control has the searchbox role, submits on Enter, and reports whether it is empty.
items.docs:
The sheet's `.ds-affix--search`. The same field anatomy as `TextField`, but on React
Aria's `SearchField`, so the control has the searchbox role, submits on Enter, and
reports whether it is empty.

```tsx
<SearchField
  value={query}
  onChange={setQuery}
  onSubmit={(term) => filter(term)}
>
  <SearchField.Label>Search monitors</SearchField.Label>
  <SearchField.Group>
    <SearchField.Icon />
    <SearchField.Input placeholder="Filter by name or URL…" />
  </SearchField.Group>
  <SearchField.Hint>
    {matches.length} of {total} monitors match
  </SearchField.Hint>
  <SearchField.Error>Enter at least two characters.</SearchField.Error>
</SearchField>
```

`SearchField.Icon` takes no children in the common case — it draws the magnifier traced
from the sheet's own SVG (same `viewBox`, radii and 1.5 stroke), and a child replaces it.
It carries no width or height, so it sizes in `cap` and tracks the field's `size` like
`Button.Icon`.

React Aria's `Input` does **not** read `SearchFieldContext`; `SearchField` supplies the
generic `InputContext`, `LabelContext`, `GroupContext`, `TextContext` and
`FieldErrorContext` instead. That is why the same slot components work in either field.

### The anatomy is shared, the slots are not

Every style constant for the legend + control + hint column lives in
`src/components/field.ts` — `FIELD`, `LABEL`, `GROUP`, `INPUT`, `HINT`, `ERROR`, `ICON`,
`FIELD_SIZES`. `TextField` and `SearchField` each define their own slot components over
those constants.

Sharing the _components_ instead would be less code, and wrong: Storybook derives the docs
import line from the subcomponent's value, so `SearchField.Label` would be documented as
`import { TextFieldLabel }`, and one component's JSDoc cannot describe two compound forms.
Thin wrappers are the price of docs that do not lie; the constants are the thing that must
not drift.

items.name: select
items.title: Select
items.description: The sheet's .ds-select, .ds-select-btn and .ds-select-menu. Opens a list over the page rather than pushing it down, and keeps the chosen value in the trigger where a form can read it back.
items.docs:
The sheet's `.ds-select`, `.ds-select-btn` and `.ds-select-menu`. Opens a list over the page
rather than pushing it down, and keeps the chosen value in the trigger where a form can read
it back.

```tsx
<Select defaultSelectedKey="https" placeholder="Choose a protocol">
  <Select.Label>Protocol</Select.Label>
  <Select.Button>
    <Select.Value />
    <Select.Icon />
  </Select.Button>
  <Select.Popover>
    <Select.AutoComplete>
      <Select.OptionList>
        <Select.Option id="http">HTTP</Select.Option>
        <Select.Option id="https">HTTPS</Select.Option>
      </Select.OptionList>
    </Select.AutoComplete>
  </Select.Popover>
  <Select.Hint>Applies to every check.</Select.Hint>
  <Select.Error>Choose a protocol.</Select.Error>
</Select>
```

| Slot                  | React Aria          | Notes                                                            |
| --------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Select`              | `Select`            | Owns the value. `size` is `sm \| md \| lg`, and `placeholder`    |
| `Select.Label`        | `Label`             | The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`                                   |
| `Select.Button`       | `Button`            | The trigger. Places the value and icon for you when bare         |
| `Select.Value`        | `SelectValue`       | The chosen option, or the placeholder. `flex-1`, so it truncates |
| `Select.Icon`         | —                   | The caret; `isLoading` swaps it for the spinner                  |
| `Select.Popover`      | `Popover`           | The menu surface                                                 |
| `Select.AutoComplete` | `Autocomplete`      | The filter scope. Draws the search box, renders no wrapper       |
| `Select.OptionList`   | `ListBox`           | The options                                                      |
| `Select.Option`       | `ListBoxItem`       | One choice, marked `[SET]` when chosen                           |
| `Select.Section`      | `ListBoxSection`    | A run of options, announced as a group                           |
| `Select.SectionTitle` | `Header`            | Its heading, in `.ds-select-group-label`                         |
| `Select.Menu`         | `Popover`+`ListBox` | Both together, for when there is nothing to search               |
| `Select.Hint`         | `Text`              | `slot="description"`                                             |
| `Select.Error`        | `FieldError`        | Renders nothing while the select is valid                        |

A select and an input line up in a column at every size, because both take their height from
the shared `--field-control-h`. The `Sizes` story asserts that rather than trusting it.

### Multiple selection, and how the value shows it

React Aria's `Select` does support multiple, but the mode is a **type parameter** defaulting to
`'single'`, so a plain `selectionMode="multiple"` is rejected by the compiler.
`SelectProps` here carries that parameter through, which makes the mode inferable from the prop
— and types `onChange` as an array of keys rather than one.

The value then comes from `ValueBase`, not from `selectedKey`: **`defaultValue` and `value` take
an array in multiple mode**, while `selectedKey`/`defaultSelectedKey` stay singular whatever the
mode. Both pairs are published on `SelectProps` for that reason.

`Select.Value` draws more than one selection as the first name plus a count — `HTTP +2` — and
falls through to React Aria untouched for the placeholder and the single case. Listing every
name is what a native multi-select does, and it fails the moment the list outgrows the trigger:
the value truncates and the ellipsis eats the one thing the trigger is for, how many are chosen.
The count is `shrink-0`, so it can never be the part that gets cut, and it drops away at one
selection rather than reading `+0`.

The count comes from `SelectStateContext` rather than from the value's render props, because a
function child has to be handed to React Aria up front, while the render props only say how many
are selected _after_ it has decided to call one. Reading the state lets the other two cases stay
React Aria's.

### A working default filter, and why it has to be explicit

React Aria's autocomplete scope has a default filter, and **it is not applied to a Select's
collection**. A scope with a search box and a list inside it, wired every way the types allow,
filters nothing — the input holds the query and the list shows every option. Only an
explicitly passed `filter` turns it on.

So `Select.AutoComplete` supplies one, rather than leaving a trap that looks like a styling
bug: `startsWith`, exported alongside `Select` for anyone who wants it directly. React Aria's
own default is a substring match, and the choice is visible on a list of monitors — `s`
surfacing every region with an `s` in it is worse than narrowing from the front. The `Search`
story pins the difference: `virginia` contains `iad1 · Virginia` but does not begin with it,
so the option drops out.

The scope also draws the search box itself — there is no separate search slot, because a scope
with nothing to type into would have no purpose. `Select.Menu` is the path for a list that
needs no searching at all.

The autocomplete's `inputValue`, `defaultInputValue`, `onInputChange`, `filter`,
`disableAutoFocusFirst` and `disableVirtualFocus` are re-declared on `Select.AutoComplete`
rather than inherited: docgen drops props declared under `node_modules`, so inheriting them
would leave the documented surface empty.

### The state that cannot be applied to the trigger

`Select` puts `data-invalid`, `data-required` and `data-open` on its **root**, while the border
they change is on the trigger — so, as with `Checkbox`, the field publishes `--field-border`
and `--field-hover` and the trigger reads them. The trigger's own hover rule is a specificity
step above its resting border, which is why an open trigger additionally retargets
`--field-hover`: otherwise hovering an open menu takes the hover colour and loses the teal.

**A select does not mark itself invalid with `aria-invalid`, and that is correct.** Its trigger
is a `<button>` with `aria-haspopup="listbox"`, and WAI-ARIA does not support `aria-invalid` on
`role="button"` — it applies to textboxes, comboboxes, switches and the like. React Aria is
right to withhold it where it sets it on a `Checkbox`. The failure still reaches assistive
tech, because `Select.Error` is wired to the trigger as its `aria-describedby`. Do not
add it back; that would be invalid markup, not a fix.

### The icon is a fixed box, not an overlay

The sheet positions its caret absolutely. Here it is a 12x12 flex child with the value on
`flex-1`, so the caret and the spinner are the same width and swapping one for the other
cannot shift the text beside them — and so neither has to know where it sits. The rotation
stays the standalone `rotate` property, driven by a variable on the root, where `data-open`
lives.

items.name: separator
items.title: Separator
items.description: The sheet's five dividers, which is why there are five.
items.docs:
The sheet's five dividers, which is why there are five.

```tsx
<Separator />
<Separator variant="strong" />
<Separator variant="dashed" />
<Separator orientation="vertical" />
```

| Variant  | Sheet            | Treatment                           |
| -------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `hair`   | `.ds-div-hair`   | `--border`, a fill                  |
| `soft`   | `.ds-div-soft`   | `--border-soft`, a fill             |
| `strong` | `.ds-div-strong` | `--foreground` — full white in dark |
| `dashed` | `.ds-div-dashed` | a `border-top`, at 45%              |
| `dotted` | `.ds-div-dotted` | a `border-top`, at 45%              |

`strong` reads `--foreground` rather than the sheet's literal `#ffffff`, because on a white page a
white rule separates nothing.

`dashed` and `dotted` are **borders**, not fills — a 1px fill cannot be dashed — and they turn with
the separator: `border-t` horizontally, `border-s` vertically, because a vertical line drawn with
`border-t` paints across a 1px column and disappears. That is the sort of thing that looks fine in a
screenshot of the wrong element.

React Aria renders it as an `<hr>` when horizontal and a `<div role="separator">` when vertical, and
it is **not** `aria-hidden`: a rule carries no text and announces nothing, so there is nothing to
hide. A first version of the story asserted `aria-hidden="true"` and was wrong.

**A separator is not a spacer.** It says two things are apart; where nothing is apart, the space is
the answer.

### Storybook forces the font size of every form control

Worth knowing before spending an hour on it. Storybook's own preview CSS contains

```css
input,
textarea,
select {
  font-size: max(16px, 1rem);
}
```

to stop iOS zooming a form on focus. That rule is **unlayered**, so it beats every Tailwind utility,
which lives in a cascade layer — and it cannot be overridden from a component without `!important`.
A textarea therefore computes **16px/24px under the test runner** while being 14px/21px in the app.

The symptom is precise and misleading: `min-height`, `padding` and `border-radius` on the same
element all apply, and only `font-size` does not. Assert the type on the **field root**, where the
field sets it, and leave the control alone.

`area.closest('[data-rac]')` does not find the root either — React Aria puts `data-rac` on every
element it renders, so the closest one is the control itself. It is `area.parentElement`.

items.name: shared-element
items.title: SharedElement
items.description: One element that moves between parents, animating from where it was to where it goes.
items.docs:
One element that moves between parents, animating from where it was to where it goes.

```tsx
<SharedElementTransition>
  {atTop ? (
    <header>
      <SharedElement name="marker" className="size-2 bg-primary" />
    </header>
  ) : (
    <footer>
      <SharedElement name="marker" className="size-2 bg-primary" />
    </footer>
  )}
</SharedElementTransition>
```

| Component                 | React Aria                | Notes                                    |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `SharedElementTransition` | `SharedElementTransition` | The scope. Renders nothing itself        |
| `SharedElement`           | `SharedElement`           | `name` is required; `isVisible` optional |

## The pair is not optional

`SharedElement` **throws** without a `SharedElementTransition` ancestor — _"`<SharedElement>` must be
rendered inside a `SharedElementTransition`"_ — which is the same shape as `ColumnResizer` without its
container. `SharedElementTransition` renders no element of its own, so it has no class list and there is
nothing to style.

## `name` is the whole contract

Render the same `name` in a different place and React Aria treats it as **one thing that moved**, carrying
its animation with it, rather than as an element that vanished and another that appeared. It reports
`data-entering` and `data-exiting` while it does, and `isVisible={false}` animates it out instead of
unmounting it.

The story proves the part that is provable in the runner: the element starts inside one parent and, after a
press, the **same element by `name`** is inside the other. The animation between those two positions is not
asserted — what is asserted is the identity that makes it possible.

## One component here already uses it internally

React Aria's own `ToggleButtonGroup` — which this repo wraps — puts a `SharedElementTransition` around its
children, so a selected segment's fill can travel rather than blink. So the machinery is already live in
this library; what this file adds is the API for a consumer laying out its own moving thing, and the
documentation of a contract that is easy to get wrong.

items.name: sheet
items.title: Sheet
items.description: A panel that slides in from an edge — a task's details without leaving the page.
items.docs:
A panel that slides in from an edge — a task's details without leaving the page.

```tsx
<Sheet>
  <Button>Details</Button>
  <Sheet.Content side="right">
    <Sheet.Title>fra1 · Frankfurt</Sheet.Title>
    <Sheet.Description>Checked every 60 seconds.</Sheet.Description>
    <Sheet.Footer>
      <Sheet.Close>Close</Sheet.Close>
    </Sheet.Footer>
  </Sheet.Content>
</Sheet>
```

| Slot                | React Aria                                | Notes                                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `Sheet`             | `DialogTrigger`                           | The trigger, then a `Sheet.Content`             |
| `Sheet.Content`     | `SheetOverlay` + `Sheet` + `SheetContent` | The scrim, the edge, and the panel              |
| `Sheet.Title`       | `Heading`                                 | The modal's own title type, imported not copied |
| `Sheet.Description` | `Text`                                    | `aria-describedby` wired here, as on `Modal`    |
| `Sheet.Footer`      | —                                         | The actions, pushed to the foot                 |
| `Sheet.Close`       | `Button`                                  | `slot="close"`, the whole mechanism             |

**A sheet is a modal that kept the page visible.** It takes the pointer and traps focus exactly as a
`Modal` does, but covers one edge instead of the middle — so the row you opened it from is still on
screen behind the scrim. Reach for `Modal` when the page is irrelevant to the decision and for this
when it is the context.

It is also a **swipe target on touch**, which is why `side` is not merely a layout prop: React Aria
resolves it into the edge _and_ the swipe direction, so a right-hand panel is dismissed by dragging
right.

## Three layers, and none of them is optional

`SheetOverlay` owns the state and draws the scrim, `Sheet` reads that state and decides the edge, and
`SheetContent` reads _its_ result. Content placed straight inside `Sheet` leaves `SheetContext` null:
`Cannot destructure property 'position' of useContext(...)` — which reads like a React bug and is a
missing layer.

**`position` is a `SheetOverlay` prop** — not `Sheet`, not `SheetContent`.

## The panel cannot be sized from outside — size the layer above it

`SheetContent` renders a `Dialog` with `style={{ width: '100%', height: '100%' }}` written _after_ the
props it is given. **An inline style outranks every class**, so a `w-96` passed to the panel does
nothing at all, and the panel is always exactly as big as the layer above it.

The size therefore goes on `Sheet`, which this component owns — `SIZES[side]` in JavaScript, where
`side` is already known. The first version put it on the panel and rendered a **250×149** panel while
the class list looked perfectly correct.

## The two earlier verdicts, revisited

This component was built, removed, and rebuilt. Both reasons it was removed are worth recording as
they turned out:

- **"It opens on load" was wrong.** A throwaway Playwright probe that navigates straight to an
  `iframe.html?viewMode=story` URL reports a dialog already open for _every_ overlay story here,
  because Storybook restores that story's canvas from a previous visit in the same browser context.
  The runner asserts the opposite: `Default`'s **first** assertion is that no dialog is present, made
  before any click, and it passes — and the click that follows opens it. That is conclusive.
- **"The panel is 250×149" was right**, and the cause was the inline style above, not a missing class.
  It now measures 384×460 in a 760×460 viewport, pinned to the right edge.

Neither was findable by reading the class list. **Read React Aria's own source for a component that
misbehaves** — `dist/private/<Name>.js.map` carries the original `tsx` in `sourcesContent`, which is how
the hardcoded `style` was found after two rounds of guessing.

## The root is `SheetTrigger`, not `DialogTrigger`

They take the same props and render the same element, and only one of them is right. React Aria's
`SheetTrigger` wraps its children in a `PressResponder` with `isPressed={false}`, in its own words to
_"prevent the trigger element from appearing stuck while the sheet is open"_. A plain `DialogTrigger`
leaves the button that opened the sheet looking pressed for as long as the sheet is up — which is exactly
what press-and-hold looks like, and is wrong.

It was found by reading React Aria's source rather than its types, because both are typed
`DialogTriggerProps` and the difference is one line of JSX.

## `SheetBackdrop` — attempted, measured, reverted

React Aria's animated scrim, which follows the panel out when a sheet is swiped. It was wired in, and the
attempt was reverted on evidence rather than on taste.

**The blocker is that React Aria owns the geometry of both layers.** A probe of the live DOM shows the
overlay reporting `position: absolute` where this component writes `fixed`, and the `Sheet` layer
reporting `relative` where it writes `absolute` — React Aria's own `sheetProps` set `position`, `top`,
`left`, `width` and `height` inline, and an inline style outranks every class. So the `Sheet` layer is
content-sized by the library, and `SheetBackdrop`'s `inset-0` can only ever resolve against **that** box.

The consequence is exact: a backdrop inside `Sheet` covers the **panel**, not the page. Making the layer
full-viewport is not a class away — it is React Aria's structure, and the first attempt collapsed the panel
from full-height to 149px, which the suite caught immediately.

The scrim therefore stays on the overlay, where it works and is tested.

items.name: slider
items.title: Slider
items.description: A value chosen by dragging a handle along a rail. The sheet has no slider in it, so this is an invention — and it is the progress bar's drawing made interactive: the same 4px rail, the same accent fill, the same progress.ts. A slider is a bar with a handle on it, and two drawings of one idea is the drift that file exists to prevent.
items.docs:
A value chosen by dragging a handle along a rail. **The sheet has no slider in it**, so this is an
invention — and it is the progress bar's drawing made interactive: the same 4px rail, the same accent
fill, the same `progress.ts`. A slider _is_ a bar with a handle on it, and two drawings of one idea is
the drift that file exists to prevent.

```tsx
<Slider defaultValue={60}>
  <Slider.Header>
    <Slider.Label>Alert threshold</Slider.Label>
    <Slider.Value />
  </Slider.Header>
  <Slider.Track>
    <Slider.Fill />
    <Slider.Thumb />
  </Slider.Track>
</Slider>
```

| Slot            | React Aria     | Notes                                                      |
| --------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Slider`        | `Slider`       | The value. `size` is `sm \| md \| lg`, and `orientation`   |
| `Slider.Header` | —              | The label and the reading on one line                      |
| `Slider.Label`  | `Label`        | Names the rail — React Aria wires it, so there is no prop  |
| `Slider.Value`  | `SliderOutput` | An `<output>`, which is the element for a control's result |
| `Slider.Track`  | `SliderTrack`  | The rail. One `Fill` and one or more `Thumb`s              |
| `Slider.Fill`   | `SliderFill`   | The filled part — the run to the thumb, or between two     |
| `Slider.Thumb`  | `SliderThumb`  | A handle. `index` and `label` for a range                  |

### A range is the same component, twice

`Slider.Track` holds as many thumbs as you write, and React Aria keeps them from crossing.
**Each thumb's accessible name is its own label _plus_ the group's** — `"From Latency window"`, not
`"From"`. That is the right answer: a screen reader crossing a form hears which window _and_ which
end of it. A story therefore matches on a prefix rather than on a name invented to make it pass.

### The handle is a grip, and it took three tries to look like one

A round thumb is what years of sliders have trained everyone to expect, and it would be a **third**
exception to a rule that has exactly two — the checkbox and the radio. A slider handle is not a
selection control; it is a grip. So it is square-cornered — literally, not by the theme's radius: it is
`rounded-none` while a button and a card take `rounded-md` and `rounded-xl` — and it grows with `size`
along with the rail.

Getting there took three attempts, and the first two are worth recording because a passing suite did
not notice either:

1. A **bordered `bg-background` square**. On the dark page that is a black box showing nothing but its own
   hairline, sitting on the rail like a rendering artifact. A border also eats a fifth of the width at
   this size.
2. A **square filled with `bg-foreground/70`**. Visible, and still wrong: a square astride a line reads as a
   bullet, not a handle.

What works is a **fader grip** — taller than it is wide, solid, in a token that already exists, with
its states moving that colour the way every other control here does: quiet at rest, full strength on
hover, and the accent only while it is actually being dragged. The accent is already spent on the
fill, so a second accent block beside it would say nothing new.

### `size` was accepted and ignored — twice

The same trap as the number field's steppers, one component later, and it survived two rounds because
the assertion only ever checked one end of it.

The first version set `h-1` outright, so `size` changed the legend's type and nothing else; `Sizes`
found three identical rails where it expected three. The rail was then wired to `--slider-rail` — and
the **handle** kept a fixed size, so three rails of three different thicknesses all carried an
identical grip, and `Sizes` still passed, because it was only looking at the rails.
`size-(--slider-thumb)` silently produced nothing; `h-(--slider-rail)` had worked the whole time.

The lesson is about the _test_ rather than the class: **check both ends of a two-ended decision.**
`Sizes` now asserts three distinct rail heights _and_ three distinct grip heights, and that every grip
is taller than it is wide.

### Disabled dims through a variable, for the fourth time

`data-disabled` is on the slider **root** while the handle is a descendant, so a
`data-[disabled]:opacity-30` on the handle never matches and the handle stayed at full strength. The
root publishes `--slider-dim` and the handle reads it — the same shape as `Checkbox`'s indicator and
`Select`'s trigger. React Aria also renders an **inner wrapper** inside the thumb, so the input's
parent is not the styled element; `data-slot="thumb"` is the hook, as it is on the fill.

### The story that matters most measures the handle

`ThumbPosition` compares the handle's centre against the rail's width and expects a quarter. That is
the whole claim a slider makes, and the one a broken layout keeps while every behavioural assertion
still passes.

## The handle: square, full-strength, and the loudest mark on the rail

| size | rail | handle |
| ---- | ---- | ------ |
| `sm` | 3px  | 16px   |
| `md` | 4px  | 20px   |
| `lg` | 6px  | 24px   |

The sheet has no slider — this is one of the components invented here — so the handle's shape and colour
were choices, and it took three readings of the rendered control to get them right.

**Shape.** It began as a `bg-background` square **with a border**, which on the dark page was a black box showing
nothing but its own hairline. The verdict was that squareness was at fault, so it became a tall narrow bar —
7×18px at `md`, then 10×24px. The next reader said it still looked wrong, rightly: a bar a hairline wide and
several rails tall reads as a **cursor**, not as something a hand closes around. The border and the black fill
were the original problem; being square never was.

**What kept it a bar was an assertion.** `Sizes` required `height > width`, annotated "that proportion is what
makes it a grip" — so the wrong shape was not merely accepted, it was _enforced_, and no amount of looking at
the component would have found that.

**Colour, which was the actual complaint.** `bg-foreground/70` is 70% white: measurably lighter than the page, but
_duller than the teal fill it sits on_ — so on the filled half of the rail the handle receded while the fill
led, and it was hard to see. It is the thing you grab; it should be the loudest mark on the rail. It is now
`bg-foreground` at full strength, which reads against both the teal fill and the dark track with no border and no ring.
Sizes moved up one step at the same time.

**The state signals are scale, not colour.** With the handle already white at rest, hover and drag have nothing
left to brighten, so they grow. Dragging used to turn the handle **teal** — the exact colour of the fill
underneath it, invisible on the filled half. The same mistake as the resting colour, found in the same pass.

All three sizes carry the same rule, and `Sizes` checks that they are still three different sizes.

items.name: sparkline
items.title: Sparkline
items.description: A single series over time with no axes and no labels — the shape of the last N readings in a table cell.
items.docs:
A single series over time with no axes and no labels — the shape of the last N readings in a table cell.

```tsx
<Sparkline data={[12, 18, 15, 24, 21, 30]} label="Requests, last 6 hours" />
```

| prop     | default | notes                                                  |
| -------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `data`   | —       | oldest first, one point per reading                    |
| `width`  | `300`   | user units **and** rendered px; a class can stretch it |
| `height` | `84`    | same                                                   |
| `label`  | —       | required; a sparkline has no other text                |

## This is the replica's own chart

`pulse-replica/js/system.js` draws it in `drawSpark`, and the dashboard uses it at `300×84` in a monitor
row while the sheet uses `306×52`. So the anatomy is copied rather than invented:

- a **teal polyline**, `stroke-width: 2`, round joins and caps;
- over a **dot-grid zone** — `rgba(255,255,255,.32)` dots, radius `0.9`, pitch `7.7px`, drawn as an SVG
  `<pattern>` because a `<rect>` cannot take a CSS background;
- the zone starting 26/84 down and stopping 14/84 short of the bottom, so it reads as a texture behind the
  trend rather than as a filled area chart;
- `preserveAspectRatio="none"`, which is what lets one component serve both sizes.

Two departures from the replica, both deliberate:

- The stroke is `var(--primary)`, not the replica's `#71FFF6`. Same colour in dark, and it follows the
  token into the light theme — the replica is dark-only and can afford a literal.
- `vectorEffect="non-scaling-stroke"` keeps the line 2px when the box is not the viewBox's aspect ratio.
  Without it, stretching a 300×84 drawing into a 300×52 cell squashes the stroke with everything else.

The replica marks its sparklines `aria-hidden`. This one carries `role="img"` and a `label`, because a
monitor's trend is the entire content of the cell and a screen reader is otherwise told nothing.

## The chart tokens it draws from

`system.css` names the pieces for the charts generally, and they are the starting point for the full chart
component:

| token         | value                   | use                      |
| ------------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `--c-bar`     | `#686d73`               | histogram bars           |
| `--line`      | `rgba(255,255,255,.62)` | hairline separators      |
| `--line-soft` | `rgba(255,255,255,.30)` | baselines, quiet strokes |
| `--dot`       | `rgba(255,255,255,.20)` | dot-grid texture         |

`.ds-dotgrid` is the same texture as a CSS background — `radial-gradient` dots on a `7.7px 7.7px` grid, with
an `--ink` variant at a heavier weight. The dashboards' chart zone also has a `.dash-axis` row: 24px tall,
labels absolutely positioned at percentages along it, and `.dash-tip--chart` for a tooltip the JS places by
writing `left`/`top`.

## The bug that a passing suite hid

The first version passed `width` and `height` only into the `viewBox`. An inline `<svg>` with a viewBox and no
CSS size **collapses to nothing** in a flex context — so the component drew a perfectly correct path into
invisible space, and a screenshot of its own Default story was an empty page.

Every assertion still passed, because they read the `d` attribute, the stroke colour and the dot zone: all
things about the _drawing_, none about the _box_. It now renders its own width and height, exactly as the
replica writes them on the element, and `Default` asserts the rendered box is 300×84 before it asserts
anything about the path. The same gap as `ToggleButton`'s off state and `TagGroup`'s remove button — **an
assertion about what was built is not an assertion about what is there.**

items.name: switch
items.title: Switch
items.description: The sheet's .ds-switch. An on/off setting, unlike a checkbox, which is one choice among several: the state reads from which side the knob sits on, and the change takes effect at once rather than on submit.
items.docs:
The sheet's `.ds-switch`. An on/off setting, unlike a checkbox, which is one choice among
several: the state reads from which side the knob sits on, and the change takes effect at
once rather than on submit.

```tsx
<Switch defaultSelected>
  <Switch.Indicator />
  <Switch.Text>Auto-retry failed checks</Switch.Text>
</Switch>
```

| Slot               | React Aria                     | Notes                                                |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `Switch`           | `SwitchField` + `SwitchButton` | Owns the state. `onChange(boolean)`, `name`, `value` |
| `Switch.Indicator` | —                              | The track and its knob, drawn for you                |
| `Switch.Text`      | —                              | The label                                            |

### `Switch` itself is deprecated

React Aria's `Switch` carries `@deprecated Use SwitchField + SwitchButton instead` in 1.22,
so this builds on that pair. `SwitchField` is the wrapper that owns the value and supplies
the validation and help-text contexts; `SwitchButton` is the `<label>` you click.
`SwitchField` renders its children directly, so a consumer would otherwise have to write the
`SwitchButton` themselves — `Switch` writes it for them, which is why the slot list has no
`Switch.Button`.

**The `<label>` is the control root, and every state lands on it** — `data-selected`,
`data-hovered`, `data-pressed`, `data-focus-visible`, `data-disabled`, `data-readonly`,
`data-invalid` and `data-required`. So the same rule as `Checkbox` applies: publish the state
on the label as custom properties and let the track read them, rather than reaching a child
through a group variant, which would tie on specificity and lose.

The `SwitchField` wrapper is a `<div>`, so `className` on `Switch` is layout only — the same
split as `TextField`, where `className` places the field and the control's own styling stays
internal.

### The edge rules are built so no two can match at once

A switch has four things that can decide its edge, and two pairs of them are not mutually
exclusive — selected and hovered, invalid and selected. Ordering those by source position
would be a coin flip, since Tailwind sorts them, so each rule is written to exclude the ones
it must not fight:

| State                  | Edge            | Specificity |
| ---------------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| rest                   | `--input`       | 1           |
| selected               | `--primary`     | 2           |
| invalid (not disabled) | `--destructive` | 3           |
| hover (not invalid/ro) | `--foreground`  | 4           |

Hover excludes invalid and read-only, so it never competes with either; invalid sits one step
above selected, so a failed switch turns red even while it is on. The fill is left alone by
the hover rule entirely: a selected switch keeps its teal and gains a rim, where a checked
checkbox inverts.

Read-only keeps its state at full strength — the knob's position is the content — and only
loses the hover, exactly as a read-only field loses its own.

Invalid turns the **edge** red rather than the fill, so an off switch shows a red ring on a
transparent track and an on switch on a teal one. A 1px ring is legible on both, which a fill
swap would not be: swapping the fill would throw away the switch's state in order to show its
error.

### Two things that make the tests lie

- **`readonly` is not a valid attribute on a checkbox input**, so React Aria does not set it.
  Assert `aria-readonly` instead — the same split as `Checkbox`.
- **The knob's travel is measured, not read off a token.** The sheet's 20px is the track's
  inner width less the knob and both 2px insets (40 − 2 − 2 − 14 − 2 = 20), so the on and off
  positions are symmetric rather than eyeballed. The test compares `getBoundingClientRect()`
  before and after, which cannot drift the way a hardcoded expectation can. And Tailwind's
  `translate-x-*` sets the standalone `translate` property, not `transform` — the same trap
  as `scale-*`.

items.title: Table
items.description: The sheet's .ds-rows and .ds-row: a panel-coloured stack separated by hairlines, closed by a softer one. The sheet builds its rows out of a CSS grid with fixed column widths, because it is laying out one dashboard; a table is a table, so the surfaces are what get borrowed.
