The sheet's `.ds-rows` and `.ds-row`: a panel-coloured stack separated by hairlines, closed by a softer one. The sheet builds its rows out of a CSS grid with fixed column widths, because it is laying out one dashboard; a table is a table, so the _surfaces_ are what get borrowed. ```tsx Monitor Status fra1 · Frankfurt Up
``` | Slot | React Aria | Notes | | -------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | `Table` | `Table` | `aria-label`; `selectedKeys`, `disabledKeys`, `selectionMode` | | `Table.Header` | `TableHeader` | The column headings | | `Table.Column` | `Column` | `isRowHeader` marks the column whose cell names the row | | `Table.Body` | `TableBody` | Takes `renderEmptyState` | | `Table.Row` | `Row` | Its `id` is what `selectedKeys` and `disabledKeys` speak in | | `Table.Cell` | `Cell` | One cell | ### The header is the table's, not the sheet's The sheet has **no table header at all**. Its rows are a dashboard grid where each cell holds its own 12px uppercase label above its value, so the row carries its labels with it. A real table says them once at the top instead, and the headings take the sheet's _quieter_ legend — 11px, spaced, 45% — rather than the full-strength treatment a row's own label gets. Row headers are the exception: the column marked `isRowHeader` is the row's identity, so it keeps full strength and everything else sits at 75%. That is styled off `[&[role=rowheader]]` on the cell, so which column identifies the row is decided once, on the column, and the styling cannot drift from it. ### Selection is a slot, and React Aria drives it `Table.Selection` is a `Checkbox` carrying `slot="selection"`. React Aria finds it by that slot and does everything else: the one in the column heading becomes select-all, and it goes **indeterminate** on its own when some rows are chosen — the `mixed` state a table needs and a plain checkbox does not have. ```tsx Monitor fra1 · Frankfurt
``` **Do not pass it `isSelected` or `onChange`** — the table supplies both through the slot, and passing them fights it. The header checkbox is labelled "Select All" by React Aria and each row's from its row header, so there is nothing to name. A selection column is a gutter, not a column: it holds a control and a heading that is itself a control, so `Table.Column` and `Table.Cell` narrow themselves to 12 units when they contain one — `has-[[data-slot=selection]]` — rather than making every table spell that out. ### No numeric variant The sheet gives its figures 16–20px, and its headline figure `--warning`. That belongs to its dashboard, where a number _is_ the point of the row. In a table it is one column of many, and a table of yellow figures is a table where nothing stands out. Pass a `className` when a column really is the point. ### A row's hover cannot be tested, so there is no story for it React Aria _does_ set `data-hovered` on a row, and it is the "correct" RAC way to style one. But it wires that to **pointer enter, which does not bubble** — so a pointer over a cell does not shade its row, and `user-event` fires its events on the target alone. The native `:hover` is no better: browsers apply it from real input only, and a synthetic event is not that. So the row's hover is the native pseudo-class — matching the sheet's `.ds-row--hover:hover` — and there is deliberately no Hover story. A story that asserts the row is opaque at rest and calls itself "Hover" would pass while testing nothing, which is worse than not having it. ### Two things the roles turned out to be - **React Aria gives a table the _grid_ roles**, not the table ones: `role="grid"` on the element, `gridcell` on the cells. So query `gridcell`, not `cell`, or the query finds nothing and the failure reads like a missing body. - **The empty state is a full-width `rowheader`.** `renderEmptyState` on the body renders a single cell with `colspan` and `role="rowheader"`, so `queryAllByRole('rowheader')` is 1 on an empty table, not 0. Assert on the message being visible and on there being no `gridcell`s. ## Resizable columns: `Table.Resizable` + `Table.Resizer` ```tsx Monitor {/* … */} …
 ``` | Slot | React Aria | Notes | | ----------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | | `Table.Resizable` | `ResizableTableContainer` | The scroll container. Required — see below | | `Table.Resizer` | `ColumnResizer` | Inside a `Table.Column`, on its trailing edge | **The two are one feature, not two props.** A `ColumnResizer` _throws_ without the container — React Aria's own message is _"Wrap your `` in a `` to enable column resizing"_. The container walks up to the first scrollable element and measures that, which is why it has to be the thing that scrolls, and why it carries `overflow-x-auto`. Column widths come from the column: `defaultWidth`, `minWidth`, `maxWidth`, or a controlled `width`. The grip shows its hairline on hover and turns **teal while the drag is live** — the accent for a genuinely active state, the same rule a selected row follows. It sits _over_ the column's trailing edge (absolute, `-end-px`) rather than taking a share of it, so widening a column never eats the neighbouring cell's padding. **Drag is the interaction and it is a pointer sequence** — pointerdown, pointermove, pointerup. A single `click` asserts nothing about it. Verified directly in the browser: dragging the Monitor grip 117px took that column from 220 to 337 and left its neighbours at 140 and 120. **The story does not assert the drag, and that is deliberate.** `userEvent.pointer` could not drive React Aria's resize here — with absolute `clientX`/`clientY` (which are accepted and then ignored when a `target` is given) or with target-relative `x`/`y` — while a real mouse does. Rather than ship an assertion that silently proves nothing, the story asserts what the runner can actually demonstrate: the column's width coming from `defaultWidth`, the grip's `role="presentation"` wrapper carrying a `type="range"` control with the column's accessible name, and the outline regression below. ### The focus ring here could never draw This column's class list carried `outline-none` next to a `data-[focus-visible]:outline-1` ring. Because `outline-none` sets Tailwind's **shared** `--tw-outline-style` — the very property every `outline-` utility reads back — the ring was unreachable: the element reported `outline-width: 1px` with `outline-style: none`. It is now a **transparent outline at rest** (`outline-1 -outline-offset-2 outline-transparent`), and `Table`'s `Resizable` story asserts exactly that, at rest, where `solid` with a transparent colour is correct and `none` is the failure. `GridList`'s row had the identical bug and the same fix; its rows now compute `2px solid` with a transparent colour. ## `Table.Footer` — the closing row ```tsx Fleet 3 monitors 98.99% ``` **A footer is not a body row that happens to be last.** It is the table's conclusion — the totals, the count, the average — and it is the one row a reader arrives at deliberately rather than scanning past. So the separation line goes _above_ it rather than below, and its type is a step quieter (`text-foreground/60`) than the data, which is the same relationship the header has at the other end. It holds `Table.Row`s like the body does, because it is the same collection machinery underneath. It renders a real **``**, after the `tbody` — and that is the assertion the story makes, because a footer drawn as a last body row looks identical and is not one. A `tfoot` written before `tbody` is legal HTML and still renders last, so the story checks the actual group order: `THEAD, TBODY, TFOOT`. ## `Table.LoadMore` — the row that asks for the next page The same sentinel as `GridList.LoadMore`, on the same shared recipe (`loadMore.tsx`). It only works inside a virtualized collection, draws nothing until `isLoading`, and **React Aria renders nothing at all for it when idle** — so a test asserts the element is absent rather than that it is empty. The mechanism, and the end-to-end proof that it fires on scroll, are in `gridlist.md` and `virtualizer.md`; this component is that machinery in another collection.

items.name: tabs
items.title: Tabs
items.description: The sheet's .ds-tabs and .ds-tabpanel: a row with one hairline under all of it, which the selected tab's indicator then sits on top of.
items.docs:
The sheet's `.ds-tabs` and `.ds-tabpanel`: a row with one hairline under all of it, which the
selected tab's indicator then sits on top of.

```tsx
<Tabs defaultSelectedKey="overview">
  <Tabs.List aria-label="Monitor detail">
    <Tabs.Tab id="overview">Overview</Tabs.Tab>
    <Tabs.Tab id="checks">
      Checks <Tabs.Count>3</Tabs.Count>
    </Tabs.Tab>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel id="overview">Everything at a glance.</Tabs.Panel>
  <Tabs.Panel id="checks">Three checks are failing.</Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>
```

| Slot          | React Aria  | Notes                                                            |
| ------------- | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Tabs`        | `Tabs`      | Owns the selection, as a single key                              |
| `Tabs.List`   | `TabList`   | The strip. Give it an `aria-label` when nothing visible names it |
| `Tabs.Tab`    | `Tab`       | Its `id` ties it to the panel                                    |
| `Tabs.Count`  | —           | The sheet's `.ds-count`, in the selected-yellow                  |
| `Tabs.Panels` | `TabPanels` | Optional wrapper around the panels                               |
| `Tabs.Panel`  | `TabPanel`  | The content behind a tab                                         |

The whole set is **one tab stop** and the arrow keys move between tabs — that is what lets a
keyboard user step past the strip rather than through it, and it wraps at both ends so the strip
is never a dead end. `Tabs.Count` is a slot rather than a number passed to `Tabs.Tab`, because a
count is often the whole reason to look at the tab and the moment it needs a dot or a colour of
its own, a prop stops being enough.

### `orientation` describes the strip

Not the panels, and not the set's overall shape. A vertical list **stacks its tabs** and moves its
hairline from the bottom edge to the trailing one, and the indicator turns with it — down the
tab's own text, 2px wide, rather than across it. Where the panel then sits is the consumer's
layout to decide; the prop has nothing to say about it.

This is easy to get half-right, and the half that is easy to miss is the strip itself: laying the
panel _beside_ the list is the obvious part and the list keeps reading as a row, announcing
itself as vertical while looking horizontal. The `Orientation` story asserts the column, the
moved hairline and the turned indicator rather than just the `aria-orientation`.

Those rules are written against the list's `aria-orientation` — `aria-[orientation=vertical]:` on
the strip, and `[[aria-orientation=vertical]_&]:` from the tab — rather than as group variants on
the tab, because a group variant ties on specificity with the tab's own rules and would leave the
outcome to source order.

### Only the selected panel is rendered

React Aria **unmounts** the unselected panels rather than hiding them, so their contents are not
in the document at all and `getByText` on an unselected panel finds nothing. A panel that needs
to hold state across a switch has to say so with `shouldForceMount`. Worth knowing before
writing an assertion about "the panel that is hidden" — there may be no such element.

### Two traps this caught

- **`transition-colors` covers `outline-color`.** The focus ring is painted through a colour
  transition, so reading it straight after focusing returns the previous colour — the same trap
  as the indicator and the knob, in a place where it is much less obvious.
- **A tab is not a field.** It gets the shared 3px ring rather than a teal border, because its
  edge is a 2px indicator that is only there when selected — there is nothing for a ring to
  repeat, which is the whole test for which of the two a control takes.

items.name: tag-group
items.title: TagGroup
items.description: The sheet's .ds-tag: a 12px uppercase chip, in the seven treatments the sheet defines — which is why there are seven.
items.docs:
The sheet's `.ds-tag`: a 12px uppercase chip, in the seven treatments the sheet defines — which is
why there are seven.

```tsx
<TagGroup aria-label="Regions">
  <TagGroup.List>
    <TagGroup.Tag id="fra1" variant="teal">
      fra1
    </TagGroup.Tag>
    <TagGroup.Tag
      id="iad1"
      variant="outline"
      href="/monitors/iad1"
      textValue="iad1"
    >
      iad1
    </TagGroup.Tag>
  </TagGroup.List>
</TagGroup>
```

| Slot             | React Aria | Notes                                    |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `TagGroup`       | `TagGroup` | The set. `selectionMode`, `disabledKeys` |
| `TagGroup.Label` | `Label`    | The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`           |
| `TagGroup.List`  | `TagList`  | The chips, wrapping                      |
| `TagGroup.Tag`   | `Tag`      | One chip. `variant`, `href`, `id`        |

| Variant                  | Sheet              | Treatment                  |
| ------------------------ | ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| _(default)_              | `.ds-tag`          | 70% text, transparent edge |
| `outline`                | `.ds-tag--outline` | an edge at 45%             |
| `teal` `gray` `yellow`   | the three fills    | the fill, carrying `ink`   |
| `outline-ring` `-yellow` | §18's two          | accent edge and text       |

### A selectable or removable chip needs an `id`

`selectedKeys` and `disabledKeys` speak in the tags' `id`s, exactly as `Table.Row` and
`Accordion.Item` do. Without one React Aria generates a key, and `defaultSelectedKeys={['fra1']}`
matches nothing: the story renders, every chip is enabled, and the assertion fails on a missing
attribute rather than on a wrong colour.

### React Aria's `Tag` is a grid row, and provides neither a link nor a remove button

It renders `div[role="row"]` inside `div[role="grid"]` — the same shape as its table and its tree —
and an `href` becomes `data-href` with nothing to click, while `onRemove` becomes
`data-allows-removing` with nothing to press. So `TagGroup.Tag` draws both from the render props: an
anchor when it has an `href`, and a `<Button slot="remove">` when the group allows removing. Same
reason `Table.Selection` writes its own slot — the one attribute that makes it work is the one nobody
remembers.

An early version wrapped every label in a `<span>`, and React Aria answered at runtime: _"A
`textValue` prop is required for `<Tag>` elements with non-plain text children."_ A chip that is not
a link now keeps its text **bare**, so the name can still be read off the markup; only a link, which
needs the wrapper, asks for `textValue`.

### The chip's hover is `:hover`, not `data-hovered`

Everywhere else in this system `data-[hovered]` is right, because React Aria supplies it. `Tag` does
not: a real pointer hover leaves the tag without the attribute, which this component's own test
found. So the chip's hover is the browser's own pseudo-class — correct for a user, and not
reproducible from the test runner. The Hover story was therefore **deleted** rather than written to
assert something else, the same call as the tooltip's hover.

### Hover deepens the tag's own colour

The sheet's `a.ds-tag:hover { filter: brightness(1.08) }` cannot survive five fills: on a near-white
yellow it is invisible, and on any of them it says nothing about _which_ tag the pointer is on. Fills
deepen toward `--ink`, the recipe the button uses; the two accented outlines have no fill to
deepen and take a wash of their own colour instead. Both derive from the base, and the `--tag-hover`
is declared by each variant and read by the base list, so the two land on the same element.

The `outline` edge is `--input` rather than the sheet's 35% white, which measures under
the 3:1 a boundary needs — the correction `--input` exists for.

## Removing a tag is your job, not the component's

**This is the part the docs left out, and it produced a chip with a working remove button that removed
nothing.** `onRemove` is not a command — it is a _report_. React Aria hands you the keys the user asked to
remove and stops there, because the group does not own the collection. A group whose handler does nothing is
a control that does nothing when pressed:

```tsx
// The story shipped this first. The button worked, the tag stayed, and the test passed.
;<TagGroup onRemove={() => {}}>…</TagGroup>

// The pattern to copy: hold the keys, and drop the removed ones.
function Regions() {
  const [keys, setKeys] = useState(['fra1', 'iad1'])
  return (
    <TagGroup
      onRemove={(removed) =>
        setKeys((cur) => cur.filter((k) => !removed.has(k)))
      }
    >
      <TagGroup.List>
        {keys.map((key) => (
          <TagItem key={key} id={key}>
            {key}
          </TagItem>
        ))}
      </TagGroup.List>
    </TagGroup>
  )
}
```

The signature is `(keys: Set<Key>) => void`, so a tag is dropped by filtering on something like
`removed.has(key)` — not by index.

### And the test that missed it

The story counted two remove buttons and checked their accessible names. Both true, both useful, and neither
one presses anything — **a remove control is only proven by the thing being gone.** The story now clicks the
first one and asserts the chip is no longer in the document, that the other one still is, and that the button
count fell. This is the same gap as `ToggleButton`'s off state: an assertion about what was _built_ rather
than about what it _does_.

items.name: text-area
items.title: TextArea
items.description: The sheet's .ds-textarea: the field anatomy with a control that takes more than one line. The third of the family, and the one field.ts was written for.
items.docs:
The sheet's `.ds-textarea`: the field anatomy with a control that takes more than one line. The
third of the family, and the one `field.ts` was written for.

```tsx
<TextArea defaultValue="" isRequired>
  <TextArea.Label>Notes</TextArea.Label>
  <TextArea.Input rows={4} placeholder="What changed?" />
  <TextArea.Hint>Markdown is fine.</TextArea.Hint>
  <TextArea.Error>Keep it under 500 characters.</TextArea.Error>
</TextArea>
```

| Slot             | React Aria   | Notes                                      |
| ---------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| `TextArea`       | `TextField`  | Owns the value. The root is a text _field_ |
| `TextArea.Label` | `Label`      | The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`             |
| `TextArea.Input` | `TextArea`   | The control. `rows` is the height          |
| `TextArea.Hint`  | `Text`       | `slot="description"`                       |
| `TextArea.Error` | `FieldError` | Renders nothing while valid                |

React Aria's `TextArea` is the **element**, not the root — so the root here is `TextField`, which is
what owns the label, the value and the validity, exactly as it does for `Input`. That is why this
shares `field.ts` rather than growing an anatomy of its own: a legend, a hairline and a hint column
do not care how many lines the answer runs to.

**There is no `size`.** A field's `size` sets a fixed control height and a textarea does not have
one; its height is its `rows`. A three-line box and a five-line box are not two sizes of the same
thing. The sheet's only variant, `.ds-textarea--compact`, is a `min-height`, which `rows` says
without a second vocabulary.

`resize-y` and never `resize-x`: making a control wider than its column is not something a user
should be able to do to a form.

items.name: text-field
items.title: TextField
items.description: The second component, and the anatomy the rest of the form controls reuse — textarea, select, checkbox and radio all want the same legend + control + hint column.
items.docs:
The second component, and the anatomy the rest of the form controls reuse —
textarea, select, checkbox and radio all want the same legend + control + hint
column.

```tsx
<TextField defaultValue="" size="md" isRequired isInvalid={taken}>
  <TextField.Label>Monitor name</TextField.Label>
  <TextField.Group>
    <TextField.Input placeholder="example.com" />
    <TextField.Icon position="start">{magnifier}</TextField.Icon>
  </TextField.Group>
  <TextField.Hint>Lowercase alphanumeric and dashes only</TextField.Hint>
  <TextField.Error>That hostname is taken</TextField.Error>
</TextField>
```

| Slot              | React Aria   | Notes                                                  |
| ----------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `TextField`       | `TextField`  | Owns `size` and the value. `onChange` gives a string   |
| `TextField.Label` | `Label`      | The sheet's `.ds-field-legend`                         |
| `TextField.Group` | `Group`      | Opt-in wrapper; the `relative` anchor for affixes      |
| `TextField.Input` | `Input`      | Height and type size come from the field               |
| `TextField.Icon`  | —            | `position="start" \| "end"`; must sit inside a `Group` |
| `TextField.Hint`  | `Text`       | `slot="description"`, so it is described-by            |
| `TextField.Error` | `FieldError` | Renders nothing while the field is valid               |

### Size travels as CSS, not context

`size` is `sm | md | lg` and sets two custom properties on the field —
`--field-control-h` and `--field-control-text` — which the control and any affix
inherit. No React context, because the affix is an ordinary descendant of the
field. A one-off override is a utility on the element rather than a new prop.

### Focus is the border, and only the border

The sheet's `.ds-input:focus` sets `outline: none` and turns the border teal.
Copy that. `Button` can carry the shared 3px-offset ring because the edge it
repeats is a solid fill; on a 1px border the same ring draws two parallel teal
hairlines with a gap between them, which reads as a rendering fault.

`outline-none` is doing real work there, not tidying up. **Chrome gives a focused
text input its `:focus-visible` ring at `outline-style: auto` regardless of React
Aria's `data-focus-visible`**, so removing our ring without disabling the UA one
just substitutes a blue browser ring on a teal system.

Focus also wins over invalid, as it does in the sheet (`:focus` out-specifies
`.ds-input--error`). Typing inside a field you have already been told is wrong is
when you least need the border shouting; the error message stays red throughout.

### Two traps, both silent

- **Always name the control's border colour.** A bare `border` utility falls back to
  `currentColor`, so a field silently grows a hairline in the text colour — white in the
  dark theme, black in the light. The sheet's `.ds-input` declares
  `border: 1px solid transparent` for the same reason; this system uses
  `border-input` instead.
- **The error state is `--destructive`, not the sheet's yellow.** The sheet had two
  accents and used yellow for warnings; here `--warning` _is_ the `secondary`
  button, so an error and a secondary action would have been the same colour.

The required marker is drawn by `TextField.Label`'s `::after` from the field's own
`data-required`, so the `*` cannot drift out of sync with `isRequired`. React Aria
puts the native `required` on the input rather than `aria-required`.

### Read-only does not dim its value

`isDisabled` dims a field to 40%, and it is tempting to give read-only the same treatment.
Don't: read-only is the one state where the value is the whole point, and at 40% the text
measures **3.42:1** — under the 4.5:1 body text needs — so the thing the user came to read
becomes the thing they cannot. The a11y check catches this; it is easy to ship otherwise,
because a dimmed field _looks_ deliberate.

Read-only keeps full-strength text and signals itself through the hairline instead, which is
the affordance it actually loses: the border goes to `--border-soft` and no longer
brightens on hover, because nothing there invites a click.

This is the same cascade problem as `Checkbox`, and it takes the same shape: `data-readonly`
is on the **field root** while the border is on the input, and a `group-data-[readonly]:`
utility ties with the input's own and loses on source order. So the field publishes
`--field-border` and `--field-hover` and the input reads them. Focus and invalid stay literal
on the input, so they outrank the published values and still win — including on a read-only
field, which remains focusable and selectable.

**Control boundaries carry a resting hairline.** `--input` is
`--foreground` at 45% — the smallest alpha that clears the 3:1 a control boundary
needs on _both_ pages (4.43:1 on the dark, 3.36:1 on the light). A control's own fill
cannot do this job: `--muted` is 1.23:1 against the dark page and 1.17:1
against the light one. Alpha compositing is not symmetric, so 40% looks adequate and
is not — 3.66:1 on black, 2.85:1 on white.

The `ControlBoundary` story checks this by compositing and measuring in both themes,
not by comparing against the token value: a token can be changed to something that
looks right and is not.

**Still open:** the `outline` button's border is the accent at 40%, which measures
2.45:1 on the dark page and 1.76:1 on the light. It needs roughly 49% and 69%
respectively, so no single alpha fixes it and raising it would visibly thicken the
button. Left alone because it is the one boundary that is arguably decorative — a
button always carries a label at full accent strength, which identifies it, whereas an
empty input has only its own edge.

items.name: time-field
items.title: TimeField
items.description: A time typed into a field — DateField's sibling.
items.docs:
A time typed into a field — `DateField`'s sibling.

```tsx
<TimeField defaultValue={parseTime('09:30')}>
  <TimeField.Label>Opens at</TimeField.Label>
  <TimeField.Group>
    <TimeField.Input />
  </TimeField.Group>
  <TimeField.Error>Enter a time.</TimeField.Error>
</TimeField>
```

| Slot              | React Aria   | Notes                                     |
| ----------------- | ------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| `TimeField`       | `TimeField`  | The value. `size`, and `granularity`      |
| `TimeField.Label` | `Label`      | The shared field legend                   |
| `TimeField.Group` | `Group`      | The bordered box the segments sit in      |
| `TimeField.Input` | `DateInput`  | The segments, drawn from the render props |
| `TimeField.Hint`  | `Text`       | `slot="description"`                      |
| `TimeField.Error` | `FieldError` | Renders nothing while valid               |

**It is `DateField` with hours and minutes instead of days.** Same slots, same `date.tsx` segments,
same field anatomy, and the same reason to exist: the segments are real, individually editable fields,
so the arrows step one of them and typing a digit advances to the next.

The two are kept as **separate compound components** rather than one with a flag, for the reason
`TextField` and `SearchField` are: Storybook derives the docs import line from the subcomponent's
value, so a shared slot would be documented under the wrong component's name. The constants they share
are the thing that must not drift — `date.tsx` and `field.ts` — and neither component owns those.

**A time field is narrow on purpose.** Two digits per segment, so the box is as wide as its contents
and no wider; stretched across a form column it reads as an empty text field rather than a filled one.

### An en-US locale adds a day-period segment

**Segments must be found by name, not by count.** `09:30` renders **three** segments in `en-US` —
hour, minute, and a day period (AM/PM) — so a "two segments" assertion counts three and fails against a
component that is working. Counting segments bakes the locale into the test.

`granularity` decides how many there are, so the same component covers a schedule and a stopwatch; both
stories look the segments up by `aria-label` instead.

items.name: toast
items.title: Toast
items.description: The sheet has no toast either — the third component here with nothing to copy, after the date picker and the accordion — so it borrows the tooltip's surface, which is the closest thing the sheet has to a floating panel, and React Aria's behaviour.
items.docs:
The sheet has no toast either — the third component here with nothing to copy, after the date
picker and the accordion — so it borrows the **tooltip's** surface, which is the closest thing the
sheet has to a floating panel, and React Aria's behaviour.

```tsx
const queue: ToastQueue<ToastData> = new Toast.Queue({ maxVisibleToasts: 3 })

<Toast.Region queue={queue} aria-label="Notifications">
  {({ toast }) => (
    <Toast toast={toast}>
      <Toast.Content>
        <Toast.Title>{toast.content.title}</Toast.Title>
        <Toast.Text>{toast.content.text}</Toast.Text>
      </Toast.Content>
      <Toast.Close />
    </Toast>
  )}
</Toast.Region>

queue.add({ title: 'Check failed' }, { timeout: 5000 })
```

| Slot            | React Aria             | Notes                                               |
| --------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `Toast`         | `UNSTABLE_Toast`       | One toast, inside a region's render function        |
| `ToastQueue`    | `UNSTABLE_ToastQueue`  | The queue itself, a class                           |
| `Toast.Region`  | `UNSTABLE_ToastRegion` | The corner they collect in. **Once**, near the root |
| `Toast.Content` | —                      | Holds the title and the text                        |
| `Toast.Title`   | —                      | The sheet's row legend, at full strength            |
| `Toast.Text`    | —                      | 13px at 70% — detail, not a second heading          |
| `Toast.Close`   | `Button slot="close"`  | `slot="close"` is what makes it the dismiss control |

### React Aria's toast is `UNSTABLE_`, and this is a thin skin over it

Every part is marked `UNSTABLE_`, and that is a real risk worth saying out loud rather than
burying at an import: the API can move between minor versions, and this component moves with it. It
was still the right trade — a queue, a region, auto-dismiss, a pause on hover, focus management and
an announcement to a screen reader are precisely what a hand-rolled toast gets wrong, and
`role="status"` on a div does not get them right.

`Toast.Close` writes `slot="close"` itself rather than leaving it to the consumer, for the same
reason `Select.Button` places its own value: the one attribute that makes it work is the one nobody
remembers, and getting it wrong still renders.

### Two consequences of the compound form

- **`Object.assign` flattens the generic**, so `toast.content` comes back as `unknown` unless the
  queue is typed at the point it is made. Hence `ToastQueue<T>`, exported as a type beside the
  component — say `new Toast.Queue<ToastData>({…})` and the rest follows.
- **`toast` is a required prop**, so there is nothing for Storybook to put in `args` and the meta
  is `as Meta<typeof Toast>` rather than `satisfies`. Every story supplies its own `render`.

`data-animation="entering" | "exiting"` is on the toast for the length of its entry and exit, so an
animation can hang off state rather than off a class that is always on. No keyframes ship with it:
which way a toast should move is a house decision.

### A toast announces itself, so it should not be the only place anything is said

It is for what has just happened and needs no answer. Anything a user must act on belongs in the
page, where it will still be there when they look back. `timeout` is how long it stays; a toast with
no timeout stays until dismissed, which is a decision worth making deliberately.

## `ToastQueue` is a named export, not a slot

Every other trailing name in this system is a component you can render — `Toast.Title`,
`Modal.Content` — so `Toast.Queue` was a name that looked renderable and was a
**React Aria class**. It is now `import { ToastQueue } from './Toast'`, and the compound contains only
components. `new ToastQueue({ maxVisibleToasts: 3 })`, then pass it to `Toast.Region`.

items.name: toggle-button
items.title: ToggleButton
items.description: A button that stays down.
items.docs:
A button that stays down.

```tsx
<ToggleButton defaultSelected>24h</ToggleButton>
<ToggleButton isSelected={live} onChange={setLive}>Live</ToggleButton>
```

| Prop         | Notes                                                      |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `variant`    | The same five the button has, because this _is_ the button |
| `size`       | The same three, from the same table                        |
| `isSelected` | Controlled or not; `onChange` gives the next state         |

**It is a button, so it wears the button's clothes.** `ToggleButton` composes `Button`'s own base
classes, variants and sizes rather than growing a second copy — the same call `field.ts` and
`popover.ts` make, except that here the shared thing was already in one file and only needed
exporting. A toggle that drifted a pixel from the button beside it would be the most visible kind of
drift there is, and `MatchesButton` measures the two against each other.

**The on-state retargets the variant's own recipe instead of painting over it.** `Button` paints
`bg-(--btn)` and derives its hover and pressed shades from it, so a selected toggle simply points
`--btn` at the accent — hover, pressed, focus and the pending spinner all follow with no second rule.
That is the same mechanism `Checkbox` and `Meter` use to move a state without replacing a colour, and
it works because a `data-[selected]:` rule outranks the plain one the variant declares, whatever order
the two land in.

**The accent, not the sheet's yellow.** `--warning` is literally named `selected-yellow`, which
makes it the obvious choice — and it is already the `secondary` button. A colour that means two things
stops meaning either, which is exactly the correction the error state needed when it moved from yellow
to red.

It is a **toggle, not a checkbox in a button's shape**: `aria-pressed` is set, so it is announced as
something that can be on or off, and it clicks off again.

## An off toggle was invisible, and nothing here could see it

`ToggleButton` composes `Button`'s base, variants and sizes — but it did **not** compose `Button`'s
`COLORS`. Every filled variant paints `bg-(--btn)`, and `--btn` is only ever set by `COLORS[color]`, so a
toggle that never applied one painted **no background at all** while `text-ink` still painted its label.
On this dark page that is black text on black: the `Default` story rendered an empty box with a focus ring
around it, and the source looked entirely correct.

**Why the tests missed it, which is the part worth keeping.** The file asserted `aria-pressed`, the
`data-selected` attribute, and the _selected_ colours — semantics, and the state that worked. The bug lived
in the one place nothing looked: the appearance of the **off** state. A suite that covers a component's
behaviour and its on-state can still be blind to whether the control is visible at all.

The fix is `color`, defaulting to `primary`, applied through the same shared `COLORS` table the button uses.
The regression test asserts the invariant directly: `default` is a filled variant, so it must paint, and
its label must not be the colour of the surface it sits on — its **own** fill if it has one, the page only
when it does not. The first version of that second assertion compared against the page alone and failed on
correct black-on-teal; comparing against the actual surface is what makes it a real check.

items.name: toggle-button-group
items.title: ToggleButtonGroup
items.description: A row of buttons where one — or several — is on. A segmented control.
items.docs:
A row of buttons where one — or several — is on. A segmented control.

```tsx
<ToggleButtonGroup selectionMode="single" defaultSelectedKeys={['24h']}>
  <ToggleButtonGroup.Button id="1h">1h</ToggleButtonGroup.Button>
  <ToggleButtonGroup.Button id="24h">24h</ToggleButtonGroup.Button>
  <ToggleButtonGroup.Button id="7d">7d</ToggleButtonGroup.Button>
</ToggleButtonGroup>
```

| Slot                       | React Aria          | Notes                                                                  |
| -------------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ToggleButtonGroup`        | `ToggleButtonGroup` | `selectionMode`, `selectedKeys`, `onSelectionChange`                   |
| `ToggleButtonGroup.Button` | `ToggleButton`      | A segment. `id` is required — a segment without one cannot be selected |

## A segment is not a `Tab`, and not a `Button`

A `Tab` swaps the panel below it. A segment changes a value the rest of the page reads. Where the sheet
has a tab row it puts an **indicator under** the current tab; here the current segment is **filled**,
because there is no panel for an indicator to point at. The fill is `--primary` with `ink` text — the
same place the accent goes on `Nav`'s current item and a selected table row.

The segments are `ghost` buttons plus two `data-[selected]:` rules, and the whole trick is that **those
rules are variants**: a variant outranks the plain `bg-transparent` / `border-transparent` the `ghost`
variant declares, whatever order the two reach the stylesheet in. `--btn` is retargeted to teal as well
as the background, so the button's own hover recipe — which deepens `--btn` toward ink — follows and the
segment deepens rather than jumping to another colour.

## The group draws the box

Every segment is border-transparent, so without the group's own border the control is a row of words
with nothing around it. The group draws the outline and each segment draws **only the divider before it**
(`[&:not(:first-child)]:border-l-line-control`), so no edge is drawn twice at the joins.

## The arrow keys do not carry the selection — but must not lose it

React Aria's model here is **manual activation**: the arrow keys move focus, and Space, Enter or a click
activates. Written into this doc originally was the tidier claim that the arrows move the selection and
wrap; the story was written, disagreed, and the doc was corrected.

The corollary is the part that matters. React Aria's own default **lets the arrow keys clear the
selection outright** — press the right arrow on a segmented control and it shows no current value at
all, which answers no question. So `single` sets `disallowEmptySelection` by default. `Keyboard`'s first
assertion is what pins that: focus has moved to the next segment _and_ the previous one is still on.

## A group has no `disabledKeys`

The prop does not exist on `ToggleButtonGroupProps` — tsc says so. A segment that cannot be turned on is
disabled on itself with `isDisabled`, which is also how a single unavailable option is expressed.

items.name: token-field
items.title: TokenField
items.description: Text with tokens inside it — a notification target, an alert's audience.
items.docs:
Text with tokens inside it — a notification target, an alert's audience.

```tsx
<TokenField
  defaultValue={
    new TokenFieldValue([
      { type: 'token', text: '#ops', value: 'ops' },
      { type: 'text', text: ' on call' },
    ])
  }
>
  <TokenField.Label>Notify</TokenField.Label>
  <TokenField.Input />
  <TokenField.Hint>
    Backspace removes the token before the caret.
  </TokenField.Hint>
</TokenField>
```

| Slot               | React Aria   | Notes                                               |
| ------------------ | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `TokenField`       | `TokenField` | The value is a `TokenFieldValue`, not a set of keys |
| `TokenField.Label` | `Label`      |                                                     |
| `TokenField.Input` | `TokenInput` | The typing surface, and where tokens are drawn      |
| `TokenField.Token` | `Token`      | Only meaningful inside `TokenField.Input`           |
| `TokenField.Hint`  | `Text`       |                                                     |

## A token is part of the value, not a chip beside it

That is the whole difference from `TagGroup`. A tag group is **a set of chips you edit as a set** —
order does not matter, each has an identity, and the control's job is to add and remove them. Here the
tokens are **words inside a sentence the user is writing**, in order, and React Aria puts the caret
between them. `TagGroup` answers _which labels apply_; this answers _who hears about it, and what do
you want to say_.

So the value is a `TokenFieldValue` — a string with tokens embedded — rather than an array of keys, and
`onChange` hands back the whole thing.

## The shape of the segments, which is not what you would guess

`TokenField.Input`'s `children` is a function, and it is called **only for tokens**:

```
case 'token':  →  children(segment)        // wrapped in zero-width spaces
case 'text':   return v.text               // a bare string, never passed to children
```

Two consequences, both of which cost a round here:

- **A text segment is not an element.** There is no node to put a `data-slot` on, and the typing
  surface's own `textContent` _is_ the sentence. So its type and colour belong on
  `TokenField.Input` — a slot for text would be dead code that looks correct in the source.
- **The parameter is typed as a token segment**, so `segment.type === 'token'` is a condition the
  compiler knows is always true. eslint says so directly: _"comparison is always true, since
  `"token" === "token"` is true"_. That lint error is the contract restated.

The zero-width spaces React Aria wraps each token in are for caret placement and are not part of what
the user sees; a test that reads the sentence has to strip them.

## No validation, and so no `Error` slot

React Aria 1.22's token field takes `isDisabled`, `isReadOnly`, `allowsNewlines` and keyboard handlers
— and **no validation props at all**: no `isInvalid`, no `isRequired`, no `validationBehavior`. An
`errorMessage` slot would render and never be wired to anything, which is worse than not having one, so
there is no `TokenField.Error`. This follows the house rule that a component is trimmed rather than
shipped broken.

## No `placeholder` either

A text field's placeholder belongs to its input element, and this container is a `role="textbox"`
`div` with none to put it on. The text content of the value is what stands in for it.

## The keyboard is most of the component

Backspace at a token's edge removes it; the arrow keys step through tokens as single characters; typing
filters what remains. None of that is implemented here, and all of it is the reason to use this rather
than compose a text field with chips.

items.name: toolbar
items.title: Toolbar
items.description: A bar of controls, walked with the arrow keys.
items.docs:
A bar of controls, walked with the arrow keys.

```tsx
<Toolbar aria-label="Range">
  <Toolbar.Group>
    <ToggleButton size="sm">1h</ToggleButton>
    <ToggleButton size="sm" defaultSelected>
      24h
    </ToggleButton>
    <ToggleButton size="sm">7d</ToggleButton>
  </Toolbar.Group>
  <Toolbar.Separator />
  <Button size="sm" variant="ghost">
    Refresh
  </Button>
</Toolbar>
```

| Slot                | React Aria  | Notes                                   |
| ------------------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `Toolbar`           | `Toolbar`   | The bar. `aria-label`, `orientation`    |
| `Toolbar.Group`     | —           | A run of controls that belongs together |
| `Toolbar.Separator` | `Separator` | The sheet's hairline, standing up       |

**The sheet has no toolbar class**, so the surface is an invention: its hairline, its square corners,
and its own controls inside it.

### One tab stop, and the arrow keys walk it

That is the whole reason to use this rather than a flex row: a bar of six controls costs a keyboard
user **one** press of Tab rather than six.

**But the toolbar itself is not focusable** — the roving tabindex lives on its children, so the entry
point is the first control. The first version of the `Keyboard` story called `bar.focus()`, and focus
stayed on the `body` with the arrow keys going nowhere. What is asserted is that the arrows move along
the row and stay inside the bar.

`Home` and `End` are **not** asserted: `End` did not reach the last control, and a test that presses a
key the component does not answer is worse than no test. That is the fourth such call here, after the
menu's type-ahead, the grid list's Space, and the breadcrumb's click.

### A segmented control is a group of toggles, and the exclusivity is the caller's

React Aria 1.22 has no `ToggleButtonGroup`, so one piece of state decides which is on. That is the
honest shape: a group of buttons is a layout, and "only one at a time" is a decision about the data
rather than about the markup.

items.name: tooltip
items.title: Tooltip
items.description: The sheet's .ds-tip — a short description attached to the thing it describes, on its own panel rather than on a themed bubble.
items.docs:
The sheet's `.ds-tip` — a short description attached to the thing it describes, on its own panel
rather than on a themed bubble.

```tsx
<Tooltip delay={0}>
  <Button>Restart</Button>
  <Tooltip.Content>
    <Tooltip.Title>Restart</Tooltip.Title>
    <Tooltip.Text>Runs the check again from the top.</Tooltip.Text>
  </Tooltip.Content>
</Tooltip>
```

| Slot              | React Aria       | Notes                                                        |
| ----------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Tooltip`         | `TooltipTrigger` | The wiring. Renders **no element** — there is no `className` |
| `Tooltip.Content` | `Tooltip`        | The surface; `delay` and placement live on the root          |
| `Tooltip.Title`   | —                | The sheet's `.ds-tip__title`                                 |
| `Tooltip.Text`    | —                | The sheet's `.ds-tip__sub`                                   |

`Tooltip` carries the thing as its first child and the tooltip as its second, so the two cannot be
wired to different things. Like `Select.AutoComplete`, the root renders no element of its own — so
it takes **no `className`**, and the class goes on the thing being described.

`Tooltip.Title` is 12px, letterspaced, `--primary`, and deliberately **not uppercase** — the one
piece of small text in this system that is not. A tooltip is read at a glance while the pointer
rests, not scanned down a column.

### A tooltip is not a label

It opens on hover and on focus, cannot be scrolled or selected, and is gone the moment the pointer
moves. Anything a user must read twice, copy, or click belongs somewhere else. React Aria supplies
what a hand-rolled tooltip always gets wrong: it opens on **focus**, so a keyboard user can reach
it; it is `aria-describedby` rather than a replacement for the element's name; Escape closes it
without moving focus; and it waits before opening on hover, so a pointer crossing a toolbar does
not flicker through every tooltip in it.

### The hover path cannot be tested here, so there is no story for it

React Aria opens a tooltip on hover through a **timer**, and the test runner's polling never
advances it. That is the trap the Testing section already records — a query that fails with
`Unable to find an accessible element with the role "tooltip"` and reads like a missing component.

Two stories were written for the hover and the delay, and both failed. The keyboard path opens
**synchronously**, so that is the one a story can prove, and `Default` and `Keyboard` both drive it
that way. The hover path is the same code; its delay is asserted nowhere rather than asserted badly.
This is the same conclusion as the table row's hover, for the same reason.

items.name: tree
items.title: Tree
items.description: A hierarchical list of items, expanded and collapsed in place.
items.docs:
A hierarchical list of items, expanded and collapsed in place.

```tsx
<Tree aria-label="Files" selectionMode="single" defaultExpandedKeys={['src']}>
  <Tree.Item id="src" textValue="src">
    <Tree.Label>src</Tree.Label>
    <Tree.Item id="index" textValue="index.ts">
      <Tree.Label>index.ts</Tree.Label>
    </Tree.Item>
  </Tree.Item>
</Tree>
```

| Slot           | React Aria        | Notes                                    |
| -------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `Tree`         | `Tree`            | The set. `selectionMode`, `expandedKeys` |
| `Tree.Item`    | `TreeItem`        | One node; nests inside itself            |
| `Tree.Label`   | `TreeItemContent` | The text, plus the disclosure            |
| `Tree.Section` | `TreeSection`     | A group                                  |
| `Tree.Header`  | `TreeHeader`      | The group's legend                       |

### It is `Nav` with the links taken out

React Aria's `NavigationTree` **extends** its `Tree`, so the two share one row vocabulary. `NAV_ITEM`,
`NAV_LEVEL`, `NAV_CHEVRON`, `NAV_LABEL`, `NAV_HEADER` and `NavCaret` are therefore **exported from
`Nav` and composed here**, not copied — a tree of files and a tree of links sit in the same sidebar and
must not drift apart. Reaching for one or the other is a decision about what a click does: this
**selects**, `Nav` **navigates**.

### The row vocabulary is `data-[current]`, and selection is not that

`Nav` says where you are with `isCurrent` → `data-[current]`. A tree says which row you chose →
`data-selected`. Sharing the constants without adding that one line left the chosen row with **no
accent at all**: it looked selected only through the browser's own text rendering, and the screenshot
showed a bright row where a teal one belonged. `Tree.Item` adds `data-[selected]:text-primary` — the same
accent, because "the one you are looking at" is the same idea in both.

### The chevron is a button with `slot="chevron"`, and React Aria insists on it

Not decoration and not negotiable. React Aria says so at runtime if it is missing — _"Expandable tree
items must contain a expand button so screen reader users can expand/collapse the item"_ — and an
earlier `Nav` drew its caret as a pseudo-element, which cannot be pressed and cannot be named.

It comes from the render props (`hasChildItems`, `isExpanded`) and is rendered **only when there are
children**, so a leaf correctly has none. `TreeItemContent` takes **no `className`**, so the classes go
on the row and on the inner elements — the same shape `Nav` already had.

### It is a treegrid, and the row carries the name

React Aria builds its tree on its table, so items are `role="row"` and labels are `role="gridcell"` —
a story querying `treeitem` finds nothing and asserts nothing. And **the cell has no accessible name**:
`Tree.Label` wraps its text in a plain `<span>` beside the chevron button, so every query here follows
the **row**. That cost a failing story against a tree that was rendering correctly.

### `defaultExpandedKeys` speaks in each item's `id`

Without one React Aria generates a key, `defaultExpandedKeys={['src']}` matches nothing, and the tree
renders fully collapsed — with no error and no warning. The same trap as `Table.Row` and
`Accordion.Item`.

## `Tree.LoadMore` — the row that asks for the next page

The same sentinel as `GridList.LoadMore`, on the same shared recipe (`loadMore.tsx`). It only works inside
a virtualized collection, draws nothing until `isLoading`, and **React Aria renders nothing at all for it
when idle** — so a test asserts the element is absent rather than that it is empty.

The mechanism, and the end-to-end proof that it fires on scroll, are in `gridlist.md` and
`virtualizer.md`; this component is that machinery in another collection.

items.name: virtualizer
items.title: Virtualizer
items.description: Renders only the rows in view.
items.docs:
Renders only the rows in view.

```tsx
import { ListLayout } from 'react-aria-components'

;<Virtualizer
  layout={ListLayout}
  layoutOptions={{ rowHeight: 44, estimatedRowHeight: 44 }}
>
  <GridList
    aria-label="Monitors"
    items={monitors}
    className="h-80 overflow-auto"
  >
    {(monitor) => (
      <GridList.Item id={monitor.id} textValue={monitor.name}>
        {monitor.name}
      </GridList.Item>
    )}
  </GridList>
</Virtualizer>
```

**A thin wrapper, and documented as one.** React Aria's `Virtualizer` takes three props — `layout`,
`layoutOptions`, `shouldObserveItemSize` — and no `className`, because it renders no chrome: the
_collection inside it_ becomes the scroll container, so the height and the overflow go on the
`GridList`. That is why this file has no class list.

## The collection must be given `items`, not mapped children

Virtualization works by React Aria building a collection and rendering only the visible slice. A `.map()`
in the consumer's JSX has already built every row by the time React sees it, which is the cost being
avoided. `items` comes from `CollectionProps`, so `GridList` has always accepted it even though nothing
here used it before.

`ListLayout` for a list, `GridLayout` for a grid, `TableLayout` for a table. `estimatedRowHeight` is what
the scrollbar is measured against before a row has ever rendered, so a wrong number shows as a jumpy
scrollbar rather than as a bug.

## Verified in a browser, not by the test runner

With **1000 monitors** the page holds **the same 11 rows** a 320px container can show — `scrollHeight`
484px rather than 44000 — measured with Playwright directly.

**The story does not assert that**, and the reason is worth recording. The Storybook test runner reports
all 1000 rows for the same story: React Aria renders the collection in full and prunes it once the scroll
container has been measured, and that pass does not happen the same way inside the runner's frame. An
assertion that passes in one environment and fails in the other is worse than none, and one loosened until
it passes in both asserts nothing.

So the story asserts what is true in either: the rows are the first monitors in order, and the list is a
**scroll container** (`overflow-y: auto`) — which is the Virtualizer's own contribution and is observable
in both. The pruning itself is recorded here as a browser measurement, and anyone changing this component
should re-measure it there.

## It is what makes `GridList.LoadMore` work

For a round the load-more sentinel was documented as a row and a spinner with no proven trigger: without a
scroll container React Aria renders **nothing** for it when idle, so there was no sentinel to observe. Put
the `GridList` inside a `Virtualizer` and it renders, watches the scroll, and calls `onLoadMore` at the end
of the list. That is the whole prerequisite, and it is asserted end to end in `Load More`.

items.name: visually-hidden
items.title: VisuallyHidden
items.description: Text for screen readers and nobody else.
items.docs:
Text for screen readers and nobody else. ```tsx Uptime — checked every 60 seconds ``` **It is not `display: none`, and it is not `visibility: hidden`.** Both of those take the text out of the accessibility tree as well as off the screen, which is the opposite of the point. This keeps the text in the tree at a clipped one-pixel box — the `sr-only` technique — so a screen reader reads it and the page does not move. The story asserts both halves, because either one alone is trivially satisfiable: the element is **visible** to the accessibility tree (`display` is not `none`, `visibility` is not `hidden`), and its box is at most one pixel in each direction with a `clip-path`. It is a component here because several others had hand-written the same `sr-only` span, and a visually hidden thing is easy to get subtly wrong: `width: 1px` without `white-space: nowrap` wraps the text into a column, and a missing `clip-path` leaves it sitting over the content it was meant to hide behind. ## It renders a `span`, not a `div` React Aria's `VisuallyHidden` defaults to a `
`. This component's whole job is to sit inside a sentence — `Uptime checked every 60 seconds` — and a block box there is both invalid HTML and a layout bug: the browser reports _"a `

` cannot contain a nested `

`"_ while the text reflows around an invisible block. The default is now `span`, which is what an inline helper should be. A consumer who genuinely needs a block can pass `elementType`. **The only evidence was a console line.** Every assertion in the story passed with the `
`, because they all measured the clip — the box, the `clip-path`, the visibility — and none of them asked what element it was. The story now asserts `tagName === 'SPAN'`. This is the fourth time in this repo that a passing suite was silent about a real defect, and the first time the defect announced itself in stderr rather than in a screenshot.
